evidence: DP World reports an estimated 50,000 tonnes of CO2e saved and an estimated 18 million road miles avoided since 2023.
Rail's share of container movements from Southampton rose from 21 per cent to 29 per cent, with five new rail services introduced.
The programme pays for import-laden containers moved by rail within 140 miles of the railhead, funded by a flat £10 fee on all import-laden containers arriving at the port.
The scheme is being extended to Rail Freight Terminal Operators through performance-based disbursements tied to quarterly targets.
plan: Set out the commercial and carbon case, noting that the company frames the aim as lower-emission options that make commercial sense for customers.

Apply McKinnon's green logistics framework to show that modal shift is one lever among several, and ask the board to confirm how the 50,000 tonnes estimate was calculated, including baseline and emissions scope.
Use modal choice to test whether rail's service is competitive beyond the 140-mile zone, comparing total logistics cost with lead time and reliability, since the article gives no service data.
Apply equity theory to the flat fee, arguing that importers who cannot shift may see the levy as unfair, which threatens the scheme's funding and continued cooperation.
Use the arcs of integration to assess whether the extension to RFTOs builds deeper collaboration or only a financial link, and recommend shared planning data alongside payments.

Recommend publishing a transparent baseline and methodology, testing additionality, reviewing the fee structure, widening service coverage, and planning how to move from a trial to a permanent arrangement.
pitfalls: Presenting the 50,000 tonnes as a verified figure rather than the company's own estimate, which the article describes as estimated.
Assuming rail is always lower-carbon than road on every route, without considering load factors, distance and the energy mix.

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that financial incentives are an effective way to shift freight from road to rail and so reduce the carbon emissions of supply chains.
outline: Explain McKinnon's levers for freight decarbonisation and where modal shift fits among them, using the Southampton programme as evidence.
Assess the cost-service trade-off that governs modal choice, and whether incentives alone can change it beyond a short radius.
Critique the reliability of the carbon claims and the fairness of the funding model, then conclude on whether the incentive can be sustained without further change.

articles.title: Trucking Rejection Rates: Why Holiday Shipping Gets SPICY
articles.takeaway: Holiday peak capacity is tightening trucking. Tender rejections are near 13 to 14 per cent and spot rates are rising for reasons other than fuel, which squeezes shippers who depend on contracted rates and reveals a labour problem behind the freight numbers.
articles.summary: A FreightWaves interview with SONAR analyst Zach Strickland forecasts that truckload tender rejection rates, which had climbed back toward 13 per cent before Thanksgiving, will rise to about 14 per cent the following week. He attributes the holiday squeeze to drivers being lost in the peak season, to drivers being limited to work within around 500 miles, and to large fleets having to persuade drivers to run during holidays, which carries a premium. Inventory levels are lower than usual, raising the risk of last-minute shipping. Spot rates are already elevated across van, refrigerated and flatbed modes, and Strickland says capacity rather than falling diesel prices is the cause. A possible port strike is expected to add only a modest bump, with larger rate effects nearer Christmas. Regional pressure points include the Midwest, Phoenix, the Gulf Coast and the Pacific Northwest, where cargo diverted from Los Angeles congestion and weather add to strain.
keyPoints: Truckload tender rejection rates rose back toward 13 per cent before Thanksgiving and are forecast to reach roughly 14 per cent the following week.
Rejection rates indicate how much pricing power carriers hold and how hard it will be to cover loads at contracted rates.
Tender volumes typically only pick up in the few days before the holiday, as many tenders are pushed out until after the break.
Drivers are lost during peak season, are limited to around 500 miles, and large fleets must persuade them to work holidays, so a premium is paid.
Inventory levels are below normal, which raises the risk of last-minute shipping and pressure on capacity.

modules.reading: This is squarely about freight transport capacity: truckload carriers, tender acceptance and the spot market for moving goods by road. In logistics operations terms, a rising rejection rate means contracted loads are not being accepted, which forces shippers onto the more expensive spot market or into delays. A logistics student should care because the article shows which lanes and modes are likely to be squeezed and why, which is the raw material for planning freight buying and service levels in peak periods.

The article describes a supply chain under stress from several directions at once: low inventory, a possible port strike, congestion at Los Angeles that diverts cargo to Seattle and Tacoma, and severe weather. These are demand, inventory and risk issues. An SCM student should note how one transport bottleneck changes routing and buffer decisions, and that the pressure is concentrated in particular lanes rather than spread evenly across the network.

Shippers buying road capacity are, in purchasing terms, buyers in a supplier-led market. The article shows carriers holding pricing power, reflected in rejection rates and in spot rates elevated across three modes, which affects whether contracted rates hold and how much a buyer pays for cover. A purchasing student should see the rejection rate as a measure of relative power and as a prompt to review how capacity is contracted and secured.

Behind the freight numbers is a people problem: drivers, particularly those in large fleets, must be persuaded to work over holidays when they would rather be with family, and the article says a premium is needed to achieve this. In People, Work and Organisations terms this concerns motivation, job design and the trade-off between pay and personal commitments. A student should see that a capacity shortage can have its roots in how work is designed and rewarded, not just in the size of the market.

applications.concept: Total logistics cost and the cost-service trade-off
applications.theory: Logistics decisions balance the total cost of moving and holding goods against the level of service delivered, and improving one usually affects the other. Service failures such as rejected or late loads carry hidden costs that must be counted when choosing between contracted and spot capacity.
applications.link: The article shows the trade-off in practice: a shipper facing rejection rates near 13 to 14 per cent must choose between paying the spot premium carriers are demanding and risking service failure on loads already tendered. Strickland's observation that many tenders are pushed out until after the break suggests that late cover is where the premium is most likely to bite. Lower inventory makes a missed delivery more damaging because there is less buffer to absorb it. The Midwest and Gulf Coast lanes, where weighted rejection rates are rising in lower-volume markets, are where this trade-off is sharpest.
applications.critique: The framework assumes the cost of a late or failed delivery can be measured, but in a holiday shortage the real cost may lie in lost customers or stock-outs that are hard to quantify. Cost-minimising models also tend to treat carriers as price-takers, whereas the article shows carriers setting the price through premiums.
applications.practice: A logistics manager should separate loads that can be planned early from those that cannot, pre-book capacity on critical lanes before the tender window closes, and set an explicit budget for spot premiums rather than paying them reactively. The expected cost of a missed delivery should be compared with the premium before a decision is made.

applications.theory: Cox argues that the balance of power between buyer and supplier depends on the relative scarcity and value of what each side controls, and on how easily each can find an alternative. Where supply is scarce and the buyer has few alternatives, the supplier holds the power, and the buyer must manage the relationship accordingly.
applications.link: The article describes carriers holding pricing power, reflected in rejection rates and in spot rates elevated across van, refrigerated and flatbed modes, which points to a supplier-dominant market. Strickland attributes the rise to capacity rather than fuel, so the scarcity lies in the supplier's resource, not in a cost the buyer can see and negotiate. Shippers with contracted rates find that a contract protects price but not availability, since carriers can still reject tendered loads. Because the pressure is strongest on Pacific Northwest and Gulf Coast lanes, the balance of power shifts lane by lane, so the buyer's strategy needs to be lane-specific.
applications.critique: Cox's model is most useful in relatively stable markets; in a short holiday peak power is temporary and contingent, so an analysis built on structural power may overstate its permanence. The article also draws mainly on one analyst's forecasts and does not report carrier or driver views.
applications.practice: A purchasing manager should check whether a rejected load triggers a cost or service penalty in existing contracts, identify lanes where the supplier market is tight, and negotiate capacity commitments or flexible volume agreements in advance rather than relying on the headline contracted rate.

applications.concept: Supply chain risk management and resilience (Christopher and Peck)
applications.theory: Christopher and Peck argue that supply chains are vulnerable to disruption, and that resilience depends on identifying risks, reducing the vulnerability of the network and building the ability to recover quickly. Resilience is built through redundancy, flexibility and visibility, not through efficiency alone.
applications.link: The article identifies several concurrent pressures: a possible port strike, congestion at Los Angeles that pushes freight to Seattle and Tacoma, atmospheric rivers and snow on West Coast and mountain routes, and below-normal inventories. Each adds to strain on the same transport capacity, showing how a network with little slack can be disrupted by events that appear unrelated. Rerouting cargo to Seattle and Tacoma is itself a resilience response, but it shifts the bottleneck, as the concern about low freight density in mountain and prairie regions shows. Strickland's view that a resolved strike would have only a modest effect suggests the immediate risk is manageable while later effects matter more.
applications.critique: The framework is designed for disruptions a firm can anticipate, yet much of the holiday pressure is seasonal and predictable, so treating it as a risk may understate its place in ordinary planning. Resilience also has a cost, since holding extra stock or spare capacity must be traded against efficiency.
applications.practice: A supply chain manager should map which lanes and ports are single points of failure, decide how much safety stock or alternative carrier capacity to hold for them, and set triggers for rerouting. Visibility of carrier rejection data and port status should inform these decisions early.

applications.theory: Vroom's expectancy theory holds that people are motivated to put in effort when they believe effort will lead to performance (expectancy), performance will be rewarded (instrumentality), and the reward is valued (valence). Motivation is the product of these three elements, so if any one is low, motivation falls.
applications.link: The article gives the mechanics of this in a trucking context. A driver who is limited to around 500 miles and would rather be at home must judge whether a holiday run is achievable (expectancy), whether the premium will actually be paid (instrumentality), and whether the premium is worth more than time with family (valence). Strickland says large fleets must convince drivers to get on the road and that a premium comes with that, which is the managerial lever in the model. The statement that drivers are lost during the peak suggests that the valence of time at home is high for many, so the premium must be large enough to outweigh it.
applications.critique: Expectancy theory assumes a calculating individual, yet drivers' decisions also depend on family obligations, fatigue and fairness, which pay alone may not address. Herzberg would add that a premium is an extrinsic, hygiene factor and may not produce lasting engagement.
applications.practice: A fleet manager should make the holiday premium clear and certain so drivers can see the link between working and pay, recognise that drivers value rewards differently (some may prefer time off to a premium), and offer schedule choices such as rotating or voluntary holiday rosters, which address valence and the sense of control at the same time.

caseStudy.scenario: A regional truckload carrier serving the Midwest has lost a number of drivers during the autumn and expects its large fleet to be asked to run loads from Thanksgiving through the Christmas peak. Shippers report that tendered loads are being rejected more often, and spot rates are above contracted levels. Drivers are restricted to working within about 500 miles of home, and managers must persuade them to take holiday runs when they would prefer to be with their families.
caseStudy.question: Advise the operations director how to secure enough drivers for the holiday peak, using theories of motivation and engagement, and critically evaluate whether a holiday premium alone will solve the problem.
evidence: Truckload tender rejection rates rose back toward 13 per cent before Thanksgiving and were forecast to reach roughly 14 per cent the following week.

Strickland attributes the holiday squeeze to drivers being lost during the peak, to a limit of around 500 miles, and to large fleets needing to persuade drivers to work when they want to be home, with a premium attached.
Spot rates were already elevated across van, refrigerated and flatbed modes, driven by capacity rather than by fuel, whose price was falling.
Many tenders are pushed out until after the break, so demand concentrates in the final days before the holiday.
plan: Define the problem: rejections show that the carrier cannot cover loads at contracted rates, and the constraint is driver supply, since the article notes that demand signals remain underwhelming.

Apply expectancy theory (Vroom) to each driver's decision to take a holiday run: test expectancy (can the run be completed within limits), instrumentality (will the premium be paid reliably) and valence (is the premium worth more than time at home).

Use Herzberg's two-factor theory to argue that the premium removes dissatisfaction but does not build commitment, and that schedule flexibility, recognition and control over rotas are motivators that can secure cover more durably.
Apply equity theory (Adams) to show that drivers will compare their holiday premium with colleagues', so the scheme must be seen as fair across the fleet.
Critically evaluate the premium-only approach: it addresses valence but not family pressure, fatigue or the 500-mile limit, and it may be costly and short-lived.

Recommend a package with a clear and certain holiday premium, voluntary or rotating holiday rosters, flexible boundaries where feasible, and early consultation with drivers, with weekly monitoring of rejection rates.
pitfalls: Treating drivers as purely money-driven and ignoring non-financial motivators such as family time and control over schedules.
Presenting the analyst's forecast of rising rejection rates as certain; a strong answer should acknowledge uncertainty and link recommendations to contingency planning.

alsoConsider: Bakker and Demerouti's job demands-resources model

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether financial incentives are an effective way for organisations to secure scarce labour during peak periods, drawing on motivation theory and an example from road freight.
outline: Define the motivation theory used, such as expectancy, equity or two-factor theory, and explain its components with precise terms.
Apply the theory to the road freight example, showing how drivers' choices about holiday work depend on expectancy, instrumentality and valence.
Evaluate the limits of pay-based motivation, including family pressure, fairness and the scope for non-financial levers such as job design and scheduling.

articles.title: Industrial Demand Is Broadening. So Is Competition for Space
articles.takeaway: Competition for industrial space is returning, so tenants who check power capacity first and decide quickly are the ones most likely to secure a building; the article links network design, scarce resources, the value of waiting and internal structure.
articles.summary: The article is a market update from Link Logistics, a large North American owner of last-mile industrial property, based on an interview with its leasing head. Demand is broadening from data centre activity, e-commerce, third-party logistics, cold storage and defence, and competition for buildings is returning, so tenants can no longer take their time. Large users are consolidating several 200,000 to 400,000 square foot buildings into single sites of about 1 million square feet, while last-mile users need infill sites close to customers. Power capacity has become the first question in many searches, ahead of square footage and location, because tenants plan for electrification and automation and need a credible timeline for capacity. Automation is still rare, with under 5% of Link's facilities automated, and the article ends by advising firms to evaluate sites earlier, ask about power first and decide faster.
keyPoints: Demand has built steadily, led by data centre activity, with e-commerce, third-party logistics, cold storage and defence also contributing.
Several tenants are now pursuing the same building, so slow decision-making is costing occupiers the space.
Large users consolidate multiple buildings into one site to reduce duplicated capital and management effort, while last-mile users favour proximity to customers.
Power capacity has overtaken labour, transport costs and rent as the first criterion, with the new baseline roughly double the older panel size.
Only a small share of facilities have automation, because costs remain high for most customers, and tenants weigh credit, lease term and landlord flexibility when closing deals.

modules.reading: In logistics operations terms, the article is about where warehouses sit, how big they are and how a network of sites is built, which is the core of freight and warehouse management. The shift from several buildings to one large hub for bulk users, against dispersed infill sites for last-mile users, is a live network design choice with cost and service consequences. Power availability and automation readiness determine whether a site can take the handling systems the operation needs. Students should see that the property market now constrains network design as much as the cost model does.

From a supply chain viewpoint, the article shows how network footprint decisions shape service levels, delivery speed and resilience. The retailers described want to be as close to consumers as possible, sometimes delivering within 30 minutes, which affects how inventory is positioned between stores and warehouses. Third-party logistics providers are presented as a flexible way to reconfigure a national network without tying up capital. Students should consider how the availability of space and power limits the supply chain strategy a firm can pursue.

Strategically, the article describes a market where access to scarce physical assets, such as grid power and well-located buildings, drives competitive position. Tenants compete for the same sites, which reflects rivalry for resources rather than customers. The speed with which a firm moves to secure a building is presented as a source of advantage. Students should use the article to test whether location and power are rare, valuable and hard to imitate.

Financially, the leasing choice is an investment decision with timing value. Tenants can wait, but the option to wait is shrinking as competitors move and the number of available buildings falls. Power that arrives in six, 12 or 18 months can be treated as a staged investment, with other facilities covering demand in the meantime. Students should see that the value of flexibility and the cost of delay are central to the decision.

applications.concept: Distribution network design: hub-and-spoke, consolidation and proximity
applications.theory: Distribution network design decides how many nodes a firm operates, where they are located and how stock and flows are routed between them. The central trade-off lies between consolidation, which reduces fixed costs and duplicated effort through fewer, larger sites, and proximity, which shortens delivery times and lowers transport cost to customers. Firms settle this balance by comparing total logistics cost against the service level they must achieve.
applications.link: Page describes large users consolidating three 200,000 to 400,000 square foot buildings into a single site of about 1 million square feet, because three buildings mean three sets of capital and management teams. Set against this, last-mile and omnichannel users move towards infill sites near customers, where location can matter more than specification, and some retailers aim to deliver within 30 minutes. The article therefore shows both ends of the network trade-off, scale for bulk flows and nearness for speed. National third-party providers sit between the two, since they can reposition their portfolios as client needs change.
applications.critique: Network models treat distance, cost and service as the variables to optimise, yet in this market the binding constraint is often whether a building with enough power can be leased at all, so the theoretically best node may be unavailable. These models also assume sites can be opened and closed freely, which the six to 18 month power timelines in the article contradict.
applications.practice: A logistics manager should model the network against the actual site pipeline, including power capacity and lead times, before committing to consolidation. Where service depends on proximity, the manager should keep a mix of large hubs and infill nodes and use third-party capacity as a flexible layer. Scenarios should test delays in power delivery as well as changes in demand.

applications.theory: A real option is the right, but not the obligation, to take a future action in an investment, such as delaying, expanding, staging or abandoning it. The option has value because uncertainty may resolve favourably and the firm can then act, and this value falls as the window to act closes. Standard net present value undervalues flexibility, so decision-makers add the option value to the static appraisal.
applications.link: The opening of the article describes tenants who could wait because looking at other options was a viable strategy, which is a deferral option that is now shrinking. Page notes that the choice set may fall from five or 10 options to one or two, and that several parties may chase the same building, so the value of waiting is used up quickly. The power point maps onto a staged option: tenants may not need full power on day one but need a credible path to it over six, 12 or 18 months. Keeping other facilities as a fallback works like a second option that protects the firm while the expansion is delayed.
applications.critique: Real options models assume that the underlying uncertainty can be quantified, yet the main risk described here is competitive, the chance that another tenant takes the building, which is hard to price. The models also treat the option holder as a price-taker, whereas the article suggests that landlords hold much of the bargaining power.
applications.practice: A finance or property manager should set an explicit decision deadline for each lease and value the option to wait against the risk of losing the building. Where power timing is uncertain, the manager should negotiate phased rights, such as expansion or power-upgrade options written into the lease. The business case should show the cost of waiting, not only the headline rent.

applications.theory: The resource-based view holds that a firm's advantage comes from its internal resources and capabilities rather than from industry structure alone. VRIO tests whether a resource is valuable, rare, costly to imitate and organised to be exploited, and only resources that pass all four tests are likely to sustain advantage. Scarce, hard-to-copy assets are therefore central to competitive position.
applications.link: Page's comments suggest that scarce physical resources now define competitive position in this market. A building with a 4,000-amp baseline, or a site close to dense consumer populations, is rare and difficult to replicate quickly, because grid capacity and planning approval cannot be secured in weeks. He also says that owners with 50 buildings in a market can offer more room to grow than an owner of a single facility, which points to portfolio breadth as a valuable resource. For a tenant, advantage comes from securing these resources before rivals do.
applications.critique: The resource-based view assumes the firm owns the resources that generate its advantage, whereas here the scarce assets sit with landlords and tenants gain access through contracts, so their advantage is leased rather than owned. The framework also says little about the speed of decision that the article identifies as decisive, and rivals could imitate the position by leasing the same nearby buildings.
applications.practice: A strategist should identify which property attributes are valuable, rare and hard to imitate for the firm's network, such as power capacity or infill location. The firm should then prioritise securing those assets through early commitments and leases that include flexibility. It should also check that its decision processes can exploit these assets quickly enough.

applications.theory: Galbraith's Star Model argues that organisational design rests on five interdependent components: strategy, structure, processes, rewards and people. These must be aligned with one another and with the environment, so a change in one element usually requires adjustments in the others. Structure is effective only when it fits the strategy it is meant to serve.
applications.link: Page describes a large user choosing to consolidate several buildings into a single facility because running three sites means three capital and management teams, so the structure is redesigned to remove duplication. Last-mile users take the opposite structural route, spreading into many infill sites close to customers, which shows strategy, here speed to consumers, driving structure. The concern that firms delay by over-analysing points to processes, which must match a strategy that depends on fast action. The customer advisory council of heads of real estate also shows how people and decision processes shape which sites are chosen.
applications.critique: The Star is largely a descriptive framework and does not indicate which component should change first or how much weight each should carry. It also assumes the organisation designs its own structure, whereas tenants here are constrained by the buildings the market offers, so structure may follow available space as much as strategy.
applications.practice: A manager applying the Star should test whether a consolidation or dispersal decision fits strategy, processes, rewards and people, not just cost. Where a firm consolidates sites, it should redesign management and decision processes so that fewer teams can act quickly. The manager should also check that reward systems encourage the speed of decision that the strategy requires.

caseStudy.scenario: A national retailer and its third-party logistics provider are reviewing their warehouse network in a market where industrial space is tightening. The retailer must decide whether to consolidate three existing buildings into one large facility or keep a set of smaller sites close to customers to support same-day delivery. The most suitable building has enough space for future automation, but its power upgrade could take 6 to 18 months, and other occupiers are already viewing it.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on whether to consolidate the network into one large facility or retain a dispersed infill network, and recommend how it should decide and secure the site. Critically evaluate the trade-offs using two relevant theories.
evidence: Large users consolidate 200,000 to 400,000 square foot buildings into single facilities of about 1 million square feet to avoid three sets of capital and management teams.
Last-mile and omnichannel users favour infill sites close to customers, where location can matter more than specification.
The new baseline for a large building is roughly 4,000 amps, against 2,000 amps previously, and power is now the first question in many searches.
Tenants may need to wait six, 12 or 18 months for power and use other facilities in the meantime.
Several customers and prospects are sometimes pursuing the same building, and those moving quicker are having better success.
plan: Define the decision and its objectives, comparing total logistics cost and service levels for each customer segment, using distribution network design.
Assess the site's power capacity and location as scarce, valuable and hard-to-imitate resources, applying VRIO from the resource-based view.
Evaluate timing by treating the option to wait as a real option, weighing the value of delay against the risk of losing the building.
Check internal fit using Galbraith's Star Model, aligning structure, processes, rewards and people with a consolidated or dispersed strategy.
Recommend a hybrid: a consolidated core for bulk flows, infill nodes for last-mile demand, power-path rights written into the lease, and a firm decision deadline.
pitfalls: Treating the decision as a simple cost comparison and ignoring power lead times and competition for the building.
Describing the theories in general terms without applying them to the retailer's specific trade-off between scale and proximity.

alsoConsider: Total logistics cost and the cost-service trade-off

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that an organisation's structure should be designed to fit its strategy and environment, using Galbraith's Star Model and one example of a firm changing its physical footprint in response to market conditions.
outline: Define the five components of Galbraith's Star Model and the principle that they must be aligned with one another and with strategy.
Apply the model to a firm's choice between consolidating sites and dispersing them, showing how strategy and the environment drive structure.
Critique the model as largely descriptive, unclear on which component to change first, and limited where external markets constrain design choices.

articles.title: Werner and Bennett turn AI dashcams toward crash prevention
articles.takeaway: Monitoring data that once only served as crash evidence is now used to coach drivers before incidents, which turns a PWO question about feedback, perception, change and trust into a practical management problem.
articles.summary: Werner Enterprises and Bennett Family of Companies, both using Motive's AI platform, have moved their truck camera and telematics data from post-crash reconstruction to prevention. Real-time in-cab alerts, same-day video review, AI-generated coaching and faster compliance decisions are the main changes described. The executives say the footage also protects drivers who are not at fault, but they also stress the need to earn and keep drivers' trust and note that legacy systems slow the rollout.
keyPoints: The fleet's camera programme moved from accident reconstruction and litigation exposure to preventing incidents through early coaching and intervention.
Real-time in-cab alerts for distracted driving go to the driver and the back office, and staff call the driver to a safe place when an alert fires.
Drivers cannot move on in their workflow until they have watched flagged footage, and the fleet says about 97% of these videos are reviewed on the day they occur.
Footage cleared a long-serving driver who had opposed the cameras; he now features in the fleet's training videos.
Hours-of-service compliance review fell from four or five minutes per event to around 30 seconds, with AI giving a recommendation and staff confirming or rejecting it.

modules.reading: In PWO terms this is control through monitoring and feedback applied to people doing largely unsupervised work. Drivers are away from their managers, so performance management moves from periodic review to continuous detection and same-day coaching. The case also shows how an individual's attitude to surveillance shapes how a change is received, and how hard evidence can change a driver's view of blame. A student should care because it links technology, motivation, perception, change and trust in one practical setting.

From a logistics operations perspective this is fleet management, where freight moves through drivers whose behaviour, hours and vehicle condition affect cost, safety and service. The article covers hours-of-service compliance, a regulatory and labour-cost matter, and links fault codes to shop visits, which affect vehicle availability. Telematics and video become operational performance data. The gains described relate to compliance time and driver safety rather than network design or routing, so the logistics link is secondary.

Strategically the article asks whether a technology platform can give a fleet competitive advantage. Werner and Bennett both use Motive's AI, so rivals can buy the same tool, and any edge must lie in how each carrier builds processes around it and how far legacy systems block integration. The claim that smaller carriers may move faster because they carry less legacy technology is a resource and capability argument. Strategy students can use it to test whether a capability is rare and hard to copy.

applications.theory: Attribution theory explains how people infer the causes of behaviour, either to internal dispositions such as carelessness or ability, or to external situations such as road conditions or other road users. Kelley's covariation model suggests people judge causes using consistency, distinctiveness and consensus information. Fundamental attribution error describes the tendency to over-attribute others' failures to disposition.
applications.link: The driver with about 20 years of experience was involved in a highway incident two weeks after the camera was installed, and the replay showed it was not his fault. The fleet's first response, the legal notice and the four days needed to resolve the matter all reflect how easily an incident is attributed to the driver before the evidence is seen. Video supplies situational evidence that overturns the default blame, much like a high-consistency, low-ambiguity observation in Kelley's model. The driver then moved from opposition to advocacy, which suggests that seeing the causes changed his attributions about the cameras and about himself.
applications.critique: Attribution theory assumes people reason from available information, but the footage is selected and framed by the fleet, which decides which events are flagged and how alerts are set, so the evidence itself carries managerial choices. Drivers may still attribute the camera programme to distrust or to management control rather than to safety.
applications.practice: A manager should use footage to separate situational from dispositional causes before any disciplinary decision and should share the replay with the driver. Clear rules on what triggers review, and who sees the footage, help to make attributions fair and consistent.

applications.concept: Goal-setting theory with feedback (Locke and Latham)
applications.theory: Goal-setting theory holds that specific and challenging goals lead to higher performance than vague goals or the instruction to do one's best. Feedback on progress towards the goal raises performance further, because it shows the gap between current and desired performance and allows effort to be redirected. Goal acceptance and self-efficacy are needed for the effect to hold.
applications.link: Same-day review, with drivers unable to proceed until they have watched a flagged event, shortens the gap between behaviour and feedback, which is the timing Locke and Latham associate with effective feedback. A driver who ran a stop sign can be coached about it while the event is still fresh rather than two weeks later. The AI-generated coaching videos and Henderson's remark that good drivers want to be great drivers suggest the feedback is aimed at a self-set standard. Specific, observable behaviours such as following distance and stop-sign compliance are the kind of goals the theory describes.
applications.critique: The theory assumes the goal is accepted and that the person controls the behaviour. Here the standards are set by the fleet and feedback is largely corrective, which can reduce self-efficacy and encourage defensive driving rather than learning. The article gives no outcome data on crash rates or on how drivers responded over time.
applications.practice: Managers should frame feedback around specific, achievable driving goals and give positive recognition as well as corrections. They should involve drivers in setting thresholds and track whether the flagged behaviours fall over time, separating coaching from discipline.

applications.concept: Kotter and Schlesinger's approaches to overcoming resistance to change
applications.theory: Kotter and Schlesinger argue that resistance to change can be overcome through education and communication, participation and involvement, facilitation and support, negotiation, manipulation and co-optation, and explicit or implicit coercion. Each has different costs and benefits, and the right choice depends on the source of resistance, the power of the resisters and the urgency of the change. Participation tends to build commitment but takes time.
applications.link: The antagonistic driver is a clear example of resistance to a new technology grounded in personal concern. Once he saw the replay that cleared him, his position changed, and the fleet then used him in training videos to tell other drivers what happened, which is a form of peer-led education and involvement. Whitson's refusal to go 'all in' and his remark that the system must earn trust point to a phased approach. Henderson's 'pick a provider and lean in' advice implies a strong top-down commitment to the change.
applications.critique: The framework tends to treat resistance as an obstacle to be managed, whereas driver resistance may reflect legitimate concerns about privacy, autonomy and fairness. Manipulation and coercion options sit uneasily with a programme that depends on trust. The article's evidence on resistance rests on one driver's story, which the executives tell.
applications.practice: Managers should involve drivers in setting alert thresholds and coaching content, use credible peers such as the driver in the training videos, and publish a clear policy on how footage will be used and not used. Coercion should be avoided in favour of explained, transparent rules.

applications.concept: Resource-based view and VRIO (Barney); dynamic capabilities (Teece)
applications.theory: The resource-based view holds that competitive advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable and organised (VRIO). Dynamic capabilities, as developed by Teece, are the firm's ability to sense opportunities, seize them and reconfigure its assets and processes as the environment changes. Advantage therefore depends on how resources are combined and renewed, not only on owning them.
applications.link: Both Werner and Bennett use the same Motive AI platform, so the tool is available to competitors and is neither rare nor hard to copy. The differences the article describes lie in how each fleet reconfigured its processes, for example by linking alerts to same-day coaching and by using AI recommendations in compliance review. Henderson's complaint that older systems limit how quickly new tools can be wired together shows how legacy assets can block reconfiguration. Whitson's point that a small fleet can run like a larger one suggests that process agility may matter more than scale.
applications.critique: Dynamic capabilities can become a catch-all explanation that is hard to test. The small-carrier advantage is a claim made by executives at a Motive-hosted panel, and the article offers no evidence that smaller fleets outperform larger ones on safety or cost.
applications.practice: A carrier should audit its legacy integration points and treat the choice of AI platform as less important than the processes built around it. It should invest in staff capability and governance so that the tool changes how decisions are made, and it should measure outcomes such as incident rates and review times.

caseStudy.scenario: A regional truckload carrier, similar to the fleets described in the article, is considering fitting AI cameras across its tractors to give real-time driver alerts and same-day coaching. Several long-serving drivers have said they feel watched, and older dispatch and maintenance systems do not connect easily with the new platform. Senior management must decide how to introduce the system and whether footage should inform disciplinary decisions.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on how to introduce AI camera coaching across the driver workforce so that safety improves while engagement and trust are maintained. Critically evaluate the risks of using the footage for discipline.
evidence: Flagged events are reviewed on the day they occur, and drivers cannot move on in their workflow until they have watched the footage.
A driver who first opposed the cameras was cleared by footage of an incident that was not his fault and now appears in the fleet's training videos.
Compliance review time for a single hours-of-service event fell from four or five minutes to around 30 seconds, with staff confirming or rejecting AI recommendations.
Bennett's safety executive says the system 'has to earn our trust, and it has to keep our trust', and warns against blind acceptance.
plan: Diagnose the shift from using footage as post-crash evidence to using it for prevention through feedback, citing the article's examples of real-time alerts and same-day coaching.
Apply attribution theory to show how footage can correct blame, and how fair, transparent rules on review and discipline help drivers to accept the system.
Apply goal-setting theory with feedback to justify timely, specific coaching on observable behaviours such as following distance, and set measures to test whether behaviour changes.
Use Kotter and Schlesinger's approaches to resistance to recommend participation, peer advocates and a phased rollout, and explain why coercion would undermine trust.

Consider psychological contract and autonomy concerns (Rousseau; self-determination theory) to assess the risk that surveillance reduces motivation and engagement, and set clear limits on how footage is used.

Recommend a phased programme with governance that starts with alerts and coaching, agrees discipline rules with drivers in advance, and tracks incident rates, review times, driver turnover and survey measures of trust.
pitfalls: Treating the reported efficiency gains and the anecdotal safety claims as proof that the programme works, when the article gives no crash-rate data.
Assuming drivers will accept monitoring because executives do, without considering autonomy, privacy and the psychological contract; the article reports management views rather than driver views.

alsoConsider: Lewin's three-step model and force field analysis

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether digital monitoring of employees, such as AI-enabled video in vehicles, improves performance, and explain how managers should introduce it without undermining motivation, fairness and trust.
outline: Explain how real-time and same-day feedback can improve performance and learning, using performance management and goal-setting theory with evidence from the article.
Assess how footage affects perception and attribution, showing how it can correct blame but can also be read as surveillance.
Evaluate the change and motivational risks, including resistance, autonomy and trust, and reach a balanced conclusion on when monitoring helps and when it harms.

articles.title: From a global electrification package to a new draft text: What happened on 19 November at COP31?
articles.takeaway: A late Presidency draft at COP31 that drops fossil-fuel references shows how control of the agenda and the threat of a veto shape multi-party negotiation, which makes it a direct case for PWO's Unit 5 on power, politics and conflict.
articles.summary: edie reports that, with COP31 close to ending, a late draft text from the Presidency has drawn wide criticism for removing explicit references to fossil fuels. The piece describes widening divisions between nations, a trimmed text that also weakens key climate targets, and parallel efforts to get round the stalled talks, including a global electrification package backed by more than 150 countries. Some delegations reportedly threaten to block consensus unless production caps and stricter financing terms are restored. Only the paywalled opening of the article was supplied, so this note relies on those headline claims and cannot cover later developments or the motives behind the changes.
keyPoints: The Presidency's late draft removed explicit references to fossil fuels and pared back key climate targets, drawing sharp criticism from observers.
Nations are in open confrontation over the final wording of the agreement, and the revised text is described as a purged document.
An electrification package backed by more than 150 countries is being pursued alongside the formal text to get round the deadlock.
Individual delegations threaten to block consensus unless production caps and stricter financing terms are restored.
Only the opening of the article was available, so the final outcome and the reasons for the deletions are not known from this source.

modules.reading: In PWO terms this is a case of power, politics and conflict in a setting where no single actor controls the outcome. The Presidency's drafting choices show how control of the text can shape what is decided at all, while delegations' threats to block consensus show power resting on the ability to veto. Students should care because the conflict is structural and driven by interests rather than personalities, so it can be analysed with Unit 5 concepts.

The subject is decarbonisation policy, which the green module treats as a regulatory and externality problem rather than a logistics one. Fossil-fuel references and production caps go to the source of emissions from energy and transport, so the negotiation shapes the regulatory environment in which freight decarbonisation takes place. The link is indirect because the article concerns international policy rather than logistics operations, so it is best used as context.

applications.theory: Lukes argues that power works in three dimensions: visible decisions made in open conflict, control of the agenda so that some issues never reach a decision, and shaping preferences so that people do not perceive a conflict. The second dimension is the most useful here, because power can be exercised by keeping a topic out of the text before the final rounds.
applications.link: The Presidency's late draft removes explicit references to fossil fuels, which is a form of agenda control: the issue is taken out of the text rather than defeated in a vote. The criticism from observers and the threats to block consensus show that the removal is contested, so the exercise of power is visible rather than hidden. The electrification package, backed by more than 150 countries outside the stalled text, suggests that other actors are trying to build an alternative agenda once the formal text has closed one down. Lukes would ask whose interests the omission serves and whether the affected parties had a voice in the framing.
applications.critique: Lukes's framework is strong at revealing hidden power but hard to test, since showing that a deletion was an exercise of power requires evidence of intent that public reporting rarely supplies. A pluralist reading would treat the removal as an ordinary negotiating move that other states can reverse.
applications.practice: A delegation facing this should map who controls each drafting stage and put alternative wording on the table in forums where it has allies. It should also press for explicit reasons for each deletion, so that agenda control becomes a debated decision rather than a quiet one.

applications.concept: Fox's unitarist, pluralist and radical perspectives on conflict
applications.theory: Fox distinguishes three frames for organisational conflict. The unitarist view treats the organisation as a single team with shared goals, so conflict signals failure; the pluralist view sees a coalition of groups with legitimately different interests, so conflict is normal and must be managed; the radical view locates conflict in structural inequality between groups.
applications.link: Open confrontation between nations over the final wording, with separate positions on production caps and financing terms, reads most naturally as pluralist: each party pursues interests it considers legitimate, and no authority can impose a single goal. A unitarist reading would treat the stalled text as a breakdown to be repaired by appealing to a common purpose, which is hard to sustain when the parties' interests conflict over fossil-fuel production. The radical lens adds that the ability to write the draft and the terms of financing reflect unequal resources, though the article offers only hints of this.
applications.critique: Fox's categories are ideal types and real negotiations mix them. A pluralist frame can underplay how far some parties hold more power than others, which the radical view would stress, and the article gives little evidence about the interests behind each delegation's position.
applications.practice: A manager facing this kind of conflict should accept that divergent interests are normal and design a process to handle them, rather than insisting on agreement from the outset. That means identifying the interests behind each position, separating a party's stated demand from its lowest acceptable outcome, and agreeing procedures for what happens when the group disagrees.

applications.theory: Thomas and Kilmann describe five ways of handling conflict, plotted on assertiveness (pursuing your own concerns) and cooperativeness (meeting the other party's concerns). The modes are competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating, and each suits different circumstances.
applications.link: Delegations threatening to block consensus unless production caps and stricter financing terms are restored are taking a competing stance, asserting their demands and relying on a veto. The electrification package, which has the support of more than 150 countries, looks more like collaboration or compromise because it seeks a shared outcome outside the stalled text. The Presidency's pruning of the text could be read as avoidance or accommodation of the most resistant parties, but the article does not say why the change was made.
applications.critique: The model describes individual styles and fits multi-party diplomacy poorly, because a party may adopt different modes towards different audiences at once. It also treats the modes as free choices, whereas national mandates may limit what delegates are able to accept.
applications.practice: A negotiator should diagnose which mode each party is using before responding, since threats call for a different response from requests for compromise. Where the relationship matters for later rounds, collaboration to find a package that meets both sides' core needs is usually more durable than a block.

applications.theory: An externality is a cost or benefit falling on people who are not party to a transaction, such as the damage done by emissions to the climate. Carbon pricing and regulation aim to bring such costs into decisions so that producers and consumers face the true cost of emissions. Caps on production are a quantity-based alternative to price-based instruments.
applications.link: The dispute over production caps is a direct argument about how to restrain emissions from fossil-fuel supply, closely linked to the removed references. Stricter financing terms concern who bears the cost of the transition, which is a distributional question tied to externalities. The electrification package points towards shifting energy use to cleaner sources, which for freight and warehousing would eventually mean electrified vehicles and equipment.
applications.critique: The article does not report the specific policy instruments under discussion, so any application to logistics is an inference. Economists also debate whether quantity caps or carbon prices are more efficient, and the negotiation may end up using both or neither.
applications.practice: A logistics operator facing this regulatory uncertainty should model scenarios with and without tighter production caps or carbon costs, then prioritise investments such as electrification that perform well under each. Following these negotiations closely gives time to plan for likely compliance costs.

caseStudy.scenario: A multilateral climate summit enters its final hours. The presiding nation circulates a late draft that removes explicit references to fossil fuels and softens key targets, and observers criticise the change. Some delegations threaten to block agreement unless production caps and stricter financing terms are restored, while a separate electrification package has gained the backing of more than 150 countries.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate how power, politics and conflict shaped this negotiation and its outcome, and advise the Presidency on how to secure a consensus that will hold.
evidence: The Presidency's late draft removed explicit references to fossil fuels and pared back key climate targets.
Observers have sharply criticised the deletion of core transition commitments.
Individual delegations threaten to block consensus unless production caps and stricter financing terms are restored.
A global electrification package has secured backing from more than 150 countries.
plan: Set out the situation and apply Lukes's second dimension of power to show how the omission from the draft shapes what can be decided.

Characterise the conflict as structural and interest-driven using Fox's pluralist perspective, explaining why divergent interests are legitimate and cannot be settled simply by appeal to a shared goal.
Diagnose each party's conflict style with the Thomas-Kilmann modes, distinguishing the competing stance of blocking delegations from the collaborative character of the electrification package.
Assess whether the conflict is functional or dysfunctional using Pondy's distinction: open confrontation may force clearer commitments, but a block would stall progress.

Recommend a route to consensus: restore a credible production and financing package, make drafting decisions transparent, and build a coalition around the electrification work, setting out the trade-offs.
pitfalls: Treating the Presidency's draft as proof of bad faith; the article reports the change and the criticism, not the motives behind it.
Describing the conflict as personal disagreement, which ignores the structural interests and unequal power that the theories are designed to capture.

alsoConsider: French and Raven's bases of power

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether conflict and power in multi-party negotiations, such as international climate talks, are best understood as a dysfunctional breakdown or as a normal feature of pluralist organisations.
outline: Define power, politics and conflict using Lukes's three dimensions and Fox's pluralist perspective, and explain how control of the agenda can shape outcomes.
Assess the functional and dysfunctional effects of open confrontation using Pondy's distinction and the Thomas-Kilmann modes, drawing on a negotiation example.
Evaluate the limits of these frameworks in a setting with many parties and unequal resources, and conclude with a justified view.

articles.title: Employers should prepare for a labor market shake-up in 2027, Indeed and Glassdoor say
articles.takeaway: A short forecast from two hiring platforms says employers should expect higher staff turnover and a weaker leadership pipeline, so people and talent policy becomes a priority. The abstract gives no figures or evidence, so the note relies on established theory to show how an employer should respond.
articles.summary: The abstract reports that Indeed and Glassdoor expect the labour market to be reshaped in 2027, and that talent leaders will face two main concerns: higher employee turnover and the need for a stronger leadership pipeline. The item is a brief news summary of a forecast, not a full report. It gives no data on the size of the turnover increase, the sectors affected, or how the forecast was produced. Its value for study lies in showing how an external labour market shift becomes an internal people-management problem that organisations must plan for.
keyPoints: The forecast comes from two hiring platforms, Indeed and Glassdoor, which see their own job-search and hiring data as a window on the market.
Talent leaders are expected to be most concerned about higher turnover in the coming year.
A second main concern is the leadership pipeline, meaning the supply of people ready to take senior and management roles.
The abstract gives no figures, sectors or methods, so the size and reliability of the predicted shake-up cannot be judged from it.
Turnover and succession are linked: losing staff can empty the pipeline, and a thin pipeline can make turnover more costly.

modules.reading: In People, Work and Organisations terms, the article is about the employment relationship being renegotiated from outside the firm, with staff more likely to leave and the organisation less able to fill senior roles from within. Turnover is an outcome of attitudes, motivation, perceived fairness and the psychological contract, while a leadership pipeline depends on development, career design and organisational culture. A student should care because the forecast shows how external labour market conditions push organisations into change, and because the response involves individual motivation, job design and culture rather than recruitment alone.

From a leadership perspective, the concern about the pipeline is a concern about how leaders are developed, selected and succeeded. Leadership theories about development, such as action-centred leadership, and about the quality of relationships between leaders and followers help explain why a thin pipeline matters: people who leave often do so because of their immediate leaders. The article therefore links the leadership module to retention and succession, which is a practical issue for any leader asked to build a team that can last.

applications.theory: The psychological contract is the set of unwritten beliefs an employee holds about the mutual obligations between themselves and their employer, such as effort in return for development, security or recognition. When employees believe the employer has failed to honour these expectations, they experience breach, which lowers commitment and increases the likelihood of leaving. The contract is shaped by what the organisation says, does and has done in the past.
applications.link: The abstract predicts higher turnover, which the psychological contract helps explain: in a tight or changing market, employees compare what they were promised with what other employers can offer, and a perceived breach may prompt them to act on the comparison. The forecast suggests that leaders should expect people to reassess their obligations and their future with the employer. The leadership pipeline concern fits here too, because staff who believe their development was promised but not delivered are the ones most likely to leave before reaching senior roles.
applications.critique: The theory is hard to measure, and its focus on individual beliefs can lead to underestimating the role of pay, external job offers and personal circumstances, which the abstract does not mention. Employers who attend only to perceived obligations may miss market-driven departures that no change in the relationship would prevent.
applications.practice: A manager should review what has been promised informally to key staff, especially on development, career paths and flexibility, and check whether those promises are being kept. Regular stay conversations can reveal early signs of breach before people start applying elsewhere.

applications.theory: Equity theory holds that people judge the fairness of their rewards by comparing the ratio of their inputs, such as effort and skill, to their outcomes, such as pay and recognition, with the ratio of relevant others. Perceived inequity creates tension, and people try to restore balance by changing their effort, altering their perception of the comparison or leaving the situation. Comparison is the key mechanism.
applications.link: In a labour market shake-up, employees have more visible comparison points, including job adverts, offers from competitors and reports about pay levels, which the abstract's forecast of higher turnover suggests will matter. An employee who sees that they could earn more elsewhere for similar inputs may conclude that their current reward is unfair and leave. The theory explains why turnover can rise even where the employer has not changed its practices, because the reference point has moved.
applications.critique: Equity theory assumes that people compare themselves in a relatively stable way, whereas in a volatile market the reference point may shift quickly and irrationally. It also says little about how far pay alone can offset other reasons for leaving, such as career progression or management quality.
applications.practice: A manager should benchmark pay and benefits for critical roles against the market and explain how reward decisions are made, so that comparisons are informed rather than rumour-driven. Where pay cannot match outside offers, the manager should look for fairness in other inputs, such as flexibility, progression and recognition, and communicate these clearly.

applications.concept: Triggers for change: internal and external triggers (PESTLE)
applications.theory: Organisational change is usually triggered by forces either outside the firm, such as political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors, or inside it, such as falling performance or a new leader. External triggers create pressure that the organisation must interpret before acting. Recognising the trigger early allows the organisation to shape its response rather than react under pressure.
applications.link: The forecast treats a labour market shake-up as a trigger for change in the people function: higher turnover and a thinner leadership pipeline are external pressures that require internal adjustment in retention, development and succession. The abstract makes clear that talent leaders are the ones who must respond, so the trigger is interpreted through people management. A student could use this to show how a market-level forecast becomes a change agenda for HR.
applications.critique: A forecast is not an event, and the abstract gives no evidence that the shake-up will happen. Responding to predicted triggers can waste resources if the forecast is wrong, and classifying triggers into internal and external categories can understate how they interact.
applications.practice: Before committing to a major programme, an HR leader should test the forecast against the organisation's own turnover data, exit reasons and pipeline figures. A staged response, with early actions that are useful even if the shake-up is mild, reduces the risk of over-committing.

applications.theory: Adair's action-centred leadership model describes leadership as the interaction of three overlapping needs: the task, the team and the individual. Effective leaders attend to all three, and the balance between them shifts with the situation. The model is widely used in leadership development because it gives managers a simple checklist for what they must do to lead.
applications.link: The concern about the leadership pipeline is a concern about individuals who must be developed to take on leadership tasks and teams. Using Adair's model, a development plan for future leaders should cover the task skills they need, the team leadership they must practise and the individual support that keeps them engaged. The abstract's combination of turnover and pipeline concerns suggests that the individual need, meaning development and retention, is where many organisations are weakest.
applications.critique: The model is descriptive and does not specify how to identify or select future leaders, nor how to balance competing needs when resources are tight. It also treats leadership as a set of behaviours, which may underplay the structural and cultural conditions that determine whether a pipeline forms.
applications.practice: A manager should map the key senior roles and identify, for each, two or three people who could take them on within a set period. Development should address the task, team and individual dimensions, with stretch assignments, team leadership responsibilities and regular one-to-one support.

caseStudy.scenario: A mid-sized professional services firm expects its staff to become more mobile over the coming year, and its partners worry that few of its managers are ready for senior roles. Exit interviews show that some of the people it most wants to keep have started to look at outside offers. The HR director has been asked to present a plan to the board.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on how the firm should respond to the expected rise in turnover and the weakness of its leadership pipeline. Critically evaluate the extent to which pay can address these problems.
evidence: Indeed and Glassdoor, as reported by HR Dive, expect a labour market shake-up in 2027.
Talent leaders are expected to see higher turnover as a major concern in the coming year.
A stronger leadership pipeline is identified as a further major concern for talent leaders.
The forecast comes from hiring platforms, which are well placed to observe job-search and hiring activity but do not themselves set out the detailed basis of the forecast in the abstract.
plan: Diagnose the situation by separating the external trigger, the expected market shake-up, from the internal problem, the firm's own turnover and pipeline gaps, using the triggers-for-change framework.
Analyse why people might leave using the psychological contract, identifying promises about development and career progression that may be at risk of breach.
Assess fairness in pay and reward using equity theory, comparing the firm's reward with market reference points and considering non-pay inputs.
Develop the leadership pipeline using action-centred leadership, mapping likely successors for critical roles and planning development across task, team and individual needs.

Evaluate the limits of pay, arguing that it can address perceived inequity but not broken promises or weak leadership, and conclude with a recommendation to combine targeted pay review with development and a clear career offer.
Recommend a phased plan with early measures such as stay interviews and a succession review, and a review point to test whether the forecast is being borne out in the firm's own data.
pitfalls: Presenting the forecast as certain. The abstract predicts a shake-up but gives no evidence of its size or timing, so the answer must treat it as a scenario to test.
Answering with generic advice on motivation or engagement without naming and applying a specific theory such as the psychological contract, equity theory or action-centred leadership.

alsoConsider: Herzberg's two-factor theory, for distinguishing hygiene factors such as pay from motivators such as development and rec
Kahn's model of employee engagement, for explaining why people withdraw from roles before they leave
Lewin's three-step model, for framing how an organisation prepares for and manages a change in its people practices

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that rising staff turnover and a weak leadership pipeline are best addressed through pay, rather than through the psychological contract, job design and leadership development.
outline: Explain how external labour market pressure becomes a turnover and succession problem for the organisation, using the triggers-for-change framework.
Apply the psychological contract and equity theory to show why pay alone may not retain key staff, and why perceived breach and fairness matter.
Evaluate the limits of the argument, including the weakness of the forecast's evidence and the role of leadership development in building a pipeline, and reach a reasoned conclusion.

articles.title: We’re Seeing the Costs of Moving Fast
articles.takeaway: The abstract links recent technology breakdowns to organisations giving too little time and resource to stress testing, which points to a people and culture question about how speed is valued against care, as well as a project and operations question.
articles.summary: The publisher's abstract argues that recent technology breakdowns suggest organisations are not spending enough time and resources stress testing their operations. Only this short abstract was supplied, so the note relies on that claim and does not assume findings from the full article.
keyPoints: The abstract links recent technology breakdowns to a shortfall in stress testing.
The stated shortfall is in both time and resources, so testing appears to be squeezed rather than simply overlooked.
The abstract frames the problem as a pattern across organisations, not a single firm's error.
The abstract's wording is suggestive ('suggest'), so the claim is an interpretation of recent events rather than a measured result.
The title, 'the costs of moving fast', implies that speed is being prioritised over checking that systems can cope with stress.

modules.reading: From the PWO perspective the abstract describes a trade-off between speed and care that is shaped by culture and norms rather than by technology alone. Whether testing gets time and resource depends on what the organisation values, what people feel able to say about risk, and how performance is measured. A student of organisational behaviour should care because it turns a technical failure into a question about culture, team climate and goal-setting. Only the abstract was available, so the link is drawn from its framing.

Stress testing is a form of verification and risk management, and in project terms it is one of the activities most often compressed when schedules tighten. The abstract's concern that testing receives inadequate time and resources maps onto the familiar pattern in which the iron triangle pressures lead teams to cut testing to hold the date. The abstract does not say whether the affected projects used agile or waterfall methods, so the speed point should not be assigned to either method without more information.

Supply chains depend heavily on operational technology, so a breakdown in those systems can disrupt flows of goods and information. Stress testing is one way to build the resilience that supply chain risk management seeks. The abstract is general and does not describe any supply chain, so this is a secondary connection.

applications.concept: Schein's three levels of organisational culture
applications.theory: Schein describes culture at three levels: visible artefacts, espoused values that people state, and basic underlying assumptions that are taken for granted and guide behaviour without being debated. Espoused values can differ from what people actually do, and the underlying assumptions are the hardest level to see and change.
applications.link: The abstract suggests that organisations are not giving stress testing adequate time and resources even though they are exposed to technology failures. This gap could indicate that speed is an espoused value that is stated openly, while the underlying assumption that testing is overhead goes unexamined. Schein's model would direct the student to look beneath the stated 'move fast' message to the assumptions that decide how much time testing receives in practice. The abstract does not report any evidence about what organisations say or assume, so this interpretation is a hypothesis to test.
applications.critique: Schein's model is difficult to apply from the outside, because assumptions can only be inferred from behaviour and are often unavailable to the people who hold them. The abstract provides no data on organisational culture, so the cultural explanation is one plausible reading among several, including budget constraints and competitive pressure.
applications.practice: A manager applying Schein would compare what the organisation says about quality and speed with what it rewards in budgets, schedules and promotions. Where stated values and actual choices diverge, the manager would name the hidden assumption, such as testing being a cost rather than protection, and address it through leadership messages, metrics and resource decisions.

applications.theory: Edmondson defines psychological safety as a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, so that members can speak up about mistakes, concerns or bad news without fear of punishment. Teams with high psychological safety are more likely to surface problems early and learn from failure. It is a property of the team's climate, not simply of individual confidence.
applications.link: The abstract's claim that testing is under-resourced implies that someone, somewhere, is deciding that testing can be shortened. In a team with low psychological safety, engineers or testers who think a release is not ready may stay silent to avoid appearing obstructive when the organisation is moving quickly. Edmondson's concept would point the student to the speaking-up behaviour that would allow a warning to reach decision-makers before a breakdown. The abstract does not describe any team, so this link is theoretical rather than evidenced.
applications.critique: Psychological safety explains whether concerns are voiced but not whether they are acted on, and a team can feel safe while still being overruled by budget or deadline pressure. It also works at team level, so it may not capture the structural decisions that set testing budgets.
applications.practice: A manager would build forums where testers can raise readiness concerns without penalty, and would make it normal to halt a release for stated reasons. They would also track whether warnings are acknowledged in decisions, since a safe climate that changes nothing will not protect the organisation.

applications.theory: Goal-setting theory holds that specific and challenging goals lead to higher performance than vague goals, provided people have the ability and commitment to pursue them and receive feedback on progress. The theory is usually used to explain how goals raise effort and persistence. Its effects depend on which goals are set, so narrow targets can focus effort on the measured outcome at the expense of unmeasured ones.
applications.link: If the abstract's organisations are judged mainly on speed of delivery, goal-setting theory predicts that effort will concentrate on meeting that target. Stress testing has effects that appear only later, so it is unlikely to be rewarded by a speed-based goal. The abstract's point that testing receives inadequate time and resources can be read as a consequence of goals that measure only what is visible. The theory predicts that balancing goals, such as reliability or incident rates, would redirect effort towards testing.
applications.critique: Goal-setting theory assumes goals are chosen carefully and that people accept them, but it does not explain how to decide which goals matter when speed and reliability conflict. The abstract gives no information about the goals used in the organisations concerned.
applications.practice: A manager applying goal-setting theory would set delivery goals alongside specific reliability goals, such as the number of tested scenarios or the incident rate after release, and would give feedback on both. The goals should be challenging but achievable, so that testing is not treated as a barrier to the speed target.

applications.concept: Project risk management and the risk register
applications.theory: Project risk management identifies, assesses, responds to and monitors risks to scope, time, cost and quality. The risk register records each risk with its likelihood, impact, owner and response, and it is reviewed through the project life cycle. Failing to treat testing as a risk response, or to record the risk of a breakdown, is a common reason projects suffer late failures.
applications.link: The abstract's concern that organisations are not giving stress testing enough time and resources suggests that a risk to operational stability is being accepted without being registered or priced. If the failure risk from untested systems does not appear in the register, the cost of testing looks like pure expense when set against schedule pressure. The abstract's framing of 'the costs of moving fast' implies that these costs are deferred to the point of failure. The abstract gives no data on how the affected organisations manage risk, so the link is an inference.
applications.critique: A risk register records only the risks people think to identify, and it can understate low-probability, high-impact failures that are hard to quantify. Risk registers also depend on the honesty of the risk owners, so they may reflect the optimism bias they are meant to control.
applications.practice: A project manager would list the failure of key systems as a named risk with its likelihood and impact, and would link the testing budget to the mitigation. The manager would present the testing cost as a risk response, with an estimate of the cost of a breakdown, so that the trade-off against speed is explicit to the sponsor.

caseStudy.scenario: A company in this position has recently suffered technology breakdowns that disrupted its operations.
