exam.question: Critically evaluate whether specific and measurable organisational targets motivate people to change their behaviour, or whether they encourage people to optimise the measured metric at the expense of the underlying aim, drawing on a current example.
outline: Explain goal-setting theory (Locke and Latham) and the conditions under which goals motivate: specificity, difficulty, acceptance and feedback.
Assess how the choice of metric and the influence of powerful actors shape which goals are set, using Lukes's three dimensions and an example such as Amazon's intensity target.

Evaluate the risk of goal displacement and conclude with practical design features for organisational targets, such as a published baseline, linked absolute and intensity measures and aligned incentives.

articles.title: The Five Barriers Keeping AI Agents Out of Supply Chain Planning
articles.takeaway: The five barriers to AI agents in supply chain planning are mostly about trust, data, governance and human-paced processes, so the real test is how authority is handed to people and systems in stages, which makes this a question of organisational behaviour as much as of technology.
articles.summary: A short piece by Mike Landry, CEO of ketteQ, argues that AI agents can recommend orders, flag shipments and contact suppliers, but that planners should extend their authority gradually. He sets out five barriers. Planners must be able to inspect the data, assumptions and reasoning behind a recommendation. Company data is often scattered, incomplete or contradictory, and AI can be used to diagnose this. Firms with several ERP systems and vendor agents need rules for how information moves and how conflicting recommendations are settled. Governance must say what an agent may do and who approves, reviews and intervenes, because people remain responsible. Approval and handoff processes designed for human speed can stretch a short task over several days. Landry recommends pilots that keep existing checks in place, that expand permissions step by step for familiar tasks under defined conditions, and that keep human review where judgement is needed. The article is written by a vendor describing its own product, Quintus, and it offers no outcome data.
keyPoints: Trust depends on planners being able to examine the data, assumptions and logic behind a recommendation, and on keeping their usual checking tools during a pilot.
AI can be used to find where records disagree, what evidence supports each finding and what needs correcting, so a pilot can test data readiness before the agent is allowed to act.
Several ERP systems and several vendors' agents require explicit rules for how information passes between them and how conflicts are resolved.
Accountability stays with people, so firms must name approvers, reviewers and intervention points even where a governance board exists.
Authority can grow in steps, for example from a planner approving each supplier email to the agent sending similar emails automatically with a daily report.

modules.reading: This is squarely about supply chain planning and execution. The article concerns how planning decisions, supplier messages and transaction data held in several ERP systems must be joined up across suppliers, manufacturers and customers. A supply chain student should read the fragmented data and the delays between messages as the core integration problem. The article also links the value of an agent to how quickly it can respond to late deliveries and changed customer orders, which is a resilience issue.

For People, Work and Organisations the article concerns how people come to accept and delegate authority to a non-human actor. It touches job design, because automating routine exchanges changes what planners do all day. It touches change management, because adoption is presented as a staged, pilot-based process that depends on trust. It also raises questions of accountability and approval structures, which are formal organisational matters. The vendor frames these as technical barriers, but the behavioural ones are at least as important.

The article describes adoption as a pilot that is widened in stages once there is evidence that it works. This is close to stage-gate governance in project management, where work moves forward only when defined criteria are met. The point that a pilot should follow a task across systems and handoffs to find where it breaks down is also a useful lesson on why projects fail at their interfaces.

applications.concept: Frohlich and Westbrook's arcs of integration
applications.theory: Frohlich and Westbrook describe the extent of supply chain integration as arcs running from suppliers to customers, which a firm can widen by linking its information and processes outwards and upwards. Wider integration, meaning shared information and joined-up processes, is associated with better performance, while integration limited to one side or one function leaves gaps. Integration therefore concerns information flows as well as physical flows.
applications.link: Landry's point that an agent must draw on information across several ERP systems and vendor platforms corresponds to the internal part of the arc, where records must be consolidated before they can be shared outwards. His account of a supplier question delayed across time zones shows the gap between information moving and decisions being made. The article's description of coordinating actions among suppliers, manufacturers and customers is the outward arc, where delays between messages slow execution. Frohlich and Westbrook's framework would ask whether the agent really widens integration or simply adds another silo.
applications.critique: The arcs model assumes that wider integration is always beneficial and measures it mainly by the breadth of links. The article suggests that faster information yields faster action only if the decision process changes too, and the model says little about internal approval practices.
applications.practice: A planning director should map which records and decisions cross each boundary and test whether the pilot follows a real order from customer request to supplier response. Gaps found should be fixed in data and process before the agent is given authority to act across them.

applications.concept: Hackman and Oldham's Job Characteristics Model
applications.theory: The Job Characteristics Model holds that five core job dimensions, namely skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback, shape three psychological states. These states in turn produce internal work motivation, satisfaction and performance. Autonomy and feedback from the work itself are the dimensions most affected when jobs are redesigned, and the strength of a person's growth need moderates how strongly they respond.
applications.link: Landry's example of a planner who first approves each supplier email and later lets the agent send similar messages with a daily report describes a shift in autonomy, with the planner moving from doing and checking to supervising by exception. The model predicts that this raises perceived responsibility, provided the planner still receives feedback on outcomes through the daily report. The article's point that routine exchanges can be automated while judgement is preserved suggests that task significance may rise, because planners concentrate on the exceptions that matter.
applications.critique: The model was developed for individually designed jobs and assumes the job holder can shape the work. In an agent-based process, autonomy may be formally granted while discretion is removed by the system, and the model does not deal with surveillance, deskilling or loss of control. Its link to satisfaction is also more contested than the model implies.
applications.practice: A manager should redesign planner roles on purpose, moving people from routine approvals towards exception handling and judgement, and should give clear feedback on what the agent did and why. The manager should then check whether skill variety and task significance have actually increased. Extending authority in steps, as the article describes, gives time to test whether the redesign works.

applications.concept: Kotter and Schlesinger's approaches to overcoming resistance to change
applications.theory: Kotter and Schlesinger identify several ways of dealing with resistance to change, including education and communication, participation and involvement, facilitation and support, negotiation, manipulation and coercion. The right approach depends on whether people lack information, have legitimate concerns or hold the power to block the change. Participation tends to work best when people hold relevant information and the change needs their commitment.
applications.link: Landry's advice that planners should compare the agent's answers with their own work, investigate discrepancies and extend trust gradually reflects participation and involvement combined with education. Letting planners identify where records disagree also draws them into diagnosing the problem rather than receiving a finished tool. The article implies that trust develops from visible evidence of how recommendations are reached, which points to reducing resistance through transparency rather than persuasion alone.
applications.critique: The framework treats resistance as an obstacle to be managed. Planners' scepticism may be a rational check on an agent that is wrong in places, so overcoming resistance could mean accepting poor recommendations. The article also says little about job security, which is often the strongest source of resistance to automation.
applications.practice: The change lead should involve planners early, including in setting the test cases and the conditions for verification, and should provide training in how the agent reasons. Concerns about changing roles and job security should be addressed openly. Resistance that reflects genuine errors should be recorded and acted on rather than managed away.

applications.concept: Dimensions of organisational structure: formalisation and chain of command
applications.theory: Organisation structure can be described along dimensions such as formalisation, the extent to which written rules and procedures govern work, and chain of command, the line of authority through which decisions pass. High formalisation and long approval chains give consistency and clear accountability, but they slow responses to change. Structural design involves deciding where each dimension should sit given the environment and the kind of work being done.
applications.link: Landry's example of a question arriving while colleagues in another time zone are asleep, followed by a wait for the right person to review and reply, shows how a chain of approval stretches a short task over days. His call to examine waiting periods and to automate routine exchanges, while keeping human review where judgement is needed, amounts to reducing formalisation for routine matters and keeping the chain of command for exceptions. The governance rules he describes, naming who approves and who intervenes, are a formal structure that the pilot must define.
applications.critique: Structural dimensions describe formal arrangements but not the informal practices that actually speed or slow work. The article's claim that delay is a process problem may depend on informal norms, which these dimensions do not capture. Burns and Stalker's distinction between mechanistic and organic organisations suggests that a shift towards responsiveness may be needed, not simply automating the existing chain.
applications.practice: A manager should map the approval chain for each recurring planning task and classify tasks as routine or judgement-based. Approval layers can then be removed for routine tasks within clear limits, while authority for exceptions stays with named people. The change should be judged against cycle time as well as output quality.

caseStudy.scenario: A consumer goods manufacturer with three separate ERP systems and suppliers in Asia plans to introduce AI agents into its planning department. The agents will recommend order changes, flag shipments at risk and email suppliers. Senior managers say the tool will save time, but several planners are worried about their roles and about the reliability of the underlying data.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate how the planning director should introduce the AI agents so that planners trust and use them, drawing on theories of job design and organisational change, and recommend an approach for the first six months.
evidence: Planners need to examine the data, assumptions and logic behind a recommendation, and a pilot should keep their existing checking tools in place.
Permission can be extended in steps, from a planner approving each supplier email to the agent sending similar emails automatically with a daily report.
A task that might take five minutes can take two or three days when it passes through approvals and time zones.
Companies with several ERP systems must join up their records and agree how agents pass information on and resolve conflicting recommendations.
plan: Define the problem by showing that the barriers in the article are behavioural and structural as well as technical, and name the five barriers of trust, data, fragmentation, governance and speed.
Apply Kotter and Schlesinger to plan participation, involving planners in designing the pilot tests and verification and addressing their concerns openly.
Apply Hackman and Oldham to redesign planner jobs, moving them from routine approvals to exception handling, and check whether autonomy, feedback and task significance have improved.
Apply the structural dimensions of formalisation and chain of command to map approvals, remove unnecessary layers for routine tasks and keep named human accountability for exceptions.
Use Frohlich and Westbrook's arcs of integration to decide which data and supplier links must be joined before the agents are given authority across them.
Recommend a staged plan: diagnose data first, run a verified pilot, extend authority through review gates and measure cycle time and planner engagement at each gate.
pitfalls: Treating the article as proof that AI agents improve performance, when it is a vendor's account with no outcome data. A strong answer should say so and suggest what evidence the company would need to collect.
Writing as if the agent could be accountable. The article says people remain responsible, so an answer should specify who approves, who reviews and who intervenes.

exam.question: To what extent are the barriers to introducing AI tools into organisational decision making behavioural rather than technical? Critically evaluate your answer using theories of job design and organisational change.
outline: Identify the technical barriers in the article, such as data quality and fragmented systems, and explain why they still shape how people behave towards the tools.
Apply job design (Hackman and Oldham) and resistance to change (Kotter and Schlesinger) to the human barriers of trust, autonomy and accountability, and note the limits of each theory.
Critically evaluate the vendor's framing of the barriers and reach a balanced conclusion supported by evidence, recommending how the balance should be tested in practice.

articles.title: Report: Asia-North America Trade Lane Presents High Risk Level
articles.takeaway: When carriers cut planned capacity rather than demand rising, shippers lose booking security and schedule reliability at the same time, so the risk is on the supply side and has to be managed through resilience, contracting and lead-time planning rather than through demand forecasts alone.
articles.summary: WiseTech Global's Trade Lane Outlook, released on 10 November, rates the Asia to North America ocean freight lane as high risk across capacity, booking acceptance, on-time performance and transit time, giving an overall high rating. The report attributes the expected tightening of capacity in the second half of November to carriers planning less capacity, not to stronger demand. Booking security risk is well above its historical average and rises towards the end of the four-week outlook, which means shippers may struggle to secure space on preferred sailings. Reliability is weak: monthly on-time performance slipped from 26.9% in September to 25.6% in October, a latest weekly figure of 27.3% is only a small improvement, and delays of eight days or more remain the most common late arrival outcome. Asia to Europe is rated high overall because of on-time and transit time risk, while Europe to North America is rated medium. The signals are built from carrier schedules, forecast supply and demand, booking acceptance rates, arrival performance and port operating indicators.
keyPoints: The four-week outlook rates Asia to North America ocean freight as high risk for capacity, booking acceptance, on-time performance and transit time, and therefore overall.
Capacity is expected to tighten in the second half of November because carriers are planning less capacity, not because demand is stronger.
Booking security risk is well above its historical average and increases towards the end of the outlook, threatening access to preferred sailings.
Monthly on-time performance fell from 26.9% in September to 25.6% in October; the latest weekly figure of 27.3% is only a modest recovery.
Delays of eight days or more are the largest arrival outcome, so prolonged lateness, not small slippage, is the main threat to lead times.

modules.reading: In supply chain terms, this is a supply-side disruption to an inbound lane, with capacity, booking security and lead-time variability all moving against the buyer at once. The risk is structural to the network rather than a single shock, so it calls for resilience measures such as buffers, alternative routes and early-warning visibility. A student of this module should care because the report is effectively an early-warning signal that can be fed into risk registers, safety stock decisions and sourcing plans.

Ocean freight on this lane is a transport mode and network question: carriers, sailings, ports and transit times determine whether freight arrives when planned. The article's measures of on-time performance and delay length are service measures that logistics managers use to judge carriers and to trade off cost against service. The student should see that the low reliability figures directly affect inventory, warehouse scheduling and service levels downstream.

For a buyer, ocean freight is a purchased service whose supply is concentrated in carriers, and when capacity tightens the balance of power shifts towards suppliers. Booking security risk describes the buyer's difficulty in obtaining the service it needs on acceptable terms. Purchasing students should consider how this affects contract structure, supplier mix and the choice between committed and spot capacity.

The report describes conditions in an industry in which suppliers of shipping capacity appear to be restricting supply. That raises questions about supplier bargaining power and whether a shift in capacity is cyclical or structural. Strategy students can use the article to test how far industry structure, rather than a single firm's choices, shapes the buyer's options.

applications.concept: Christopher and Peck's supply chain risk management and resilience framework
applications.theory: Supply chain resilience is the ability of a supply chain to recover from disruption and return to its original state or a better one. The framework runs from identifying supply chain risks and their sources of vulnerability, through assessing their impact, to building resilience through measures such as redundancy, flexibility, visibility and collaboration. Vulnerability is greatest where the chain is long, lean and dependent on a few sources.
applications.link: The report describes a disruption that originates with carriers reducing planned capacity, which is a supply-side source of risk that a buyer does not control. Booking security risk above its historical average shows the vulnerability is already visible in the system, not just forecast. The persistent low on-time performance and the prevalence of delays of eight days or more show that the risk affects lead times across the whole lane, so it is systemic rather than isolated. The outlook's signals function as the visibility element of the framework, allowing a buyer to see risk building before it reaches the warehouse.
applications.critique: The framework assumes the focal firm can afford to buy redundancy, but a shipper with limited volume cannot easily secure spare vessel capacity, and extra buffers conflict with the lean efficiency many firms are trying to protect. Visibility also depends on data that is often only available to the carrier or the forwarder.
applications.practice: A manager should map which products and customers depend on the Asia to North America lane and how long a stock-out would take to recover. They should then combine safety stock or earlier ordering for the most critical lines with a second carrier or routing option, and use the four-week signals as triggers to review those positions.

applications.concept: Logistics service measures and the cost-service trade-off (on-time in-full and total logistics cost)
applications.theory: Logistics performance is usually judged on service measures such as on-time in-full delivery, alongside total logistics cost, which includes transport, inventory and the cost of poor service. Managers trade cost against service by choosing modes, carriers and inventory levels, and they should aim for the combination that minimises total cost for the required service level rather than minimising transport cost alone.
applications.link: The article reports on-time performance of about a quarter of arrivals in recent months, which means the large majority of shipments on this lane arrive late against plan. The fact that delays of eight days or more are the most common late outcome matters because the cost of a late delivery depends on how long it is, not only whether it is late. A low on-time rate therefore pushes shippers towards holding more inventory or paying for faster alternatives, which increases total logistics cost even if the freight rate itself is unchanged.
applications.critique: On-time performance based on carrier schedules can hide differences between carriers, ports and product types, and a single weekly figure can mislead. Total cost models also depend on estimates of the cost of a stock-out, which are hard to measure, so the apparent trade-off can be imprecise.
applications.practice: A logistics manager should track on-time in-full by carrier, port and product, rather than relying on the headline lane figure. Where the cost of delay is high, they should compare the total cost of extra safety stock, air or alternative port routings with the expected cost of late arrival, and choose the option that meets the required service level at least cost.

applications.theory: Cox argues that the balance of power between buyer and supplier depends on the relative dependence each has on the other, which is shaped by the scarcity of what is supplied, the switching costs and the number of alternatives available. Where the supplier has the advantage, the buyer has to accept worse terms or manage the relationship more carefully. The buyer's power is greatest where the supply is plentiful and easy to switch.
applications.link: The report suggests that the balance has moved towards carriers, since capacity is tightening because planned supply falls, and booking acceptance is weak, so buyers find it harder to secure preferred sailings. The emphasis on securing space on preferred sailings shows that the buyer's need for specific capacity gives the carrier leverage. The fact that the shortage is driven by carrier decisions rather than demand means the buyer cannot simply wait for demand to fall to restore its position.
applications.critique: Cox's analysis is largely relational and assumes a fairly stable set of suppliers, whereas ocean freight has many carriers and a spot market in which volume can be moved quickly. The buyer's power may therefore be greater than the report implies if it can spread volume across carriers, although that depends on how much capacity is actually available elsewhere.
applications.practice: Purchasing managers should reassess ocean freight as a supply market where capacity is constrained, and look to reduce their dependence by negotiating capacity commitments, spreading volume across carriers and developing a spot-market fallback. They should also use the outlook to time contract renewals so they do not negotiate during the tightest period.

applications.theory: Porter's five forces model describes the competitive structure of an industry through five pressures: rivalry among existing firms, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitutes, and the bargaining power of buyers and suppliers. Industries are more profitable and their firms have more control where suppliers and buyers are weak and entry and substitution are limited.
applications.link: In this case the relevant pressure is the bargaining power of suppliers, here carriers that provide shipping capacity. The report indicates that carriers are reducing planned capacity, which strengthens their position relative to buyers whose booking security is falling. Capacity cuts can also be read as a sign of rivalry being moderated among carriers, since the reduction in supply supports pricing and the carriers' own position.
applications.critique: The five forces model is a static, industry-level analysis and does not explain why carriers have reduced capacity or whether they will keep doing so. The report describes a short-term outlook, so a five forces view could overstate a cyclical shift as a permanent change in industry structure.
applications.practice: A strategy team should test whether the change in capacity is cyclical or structural by looking at how long carrier capacity restraint has persisted and how it compares with historical patterns. If it appears structural, the firm should consider longer-term responses such as partnering with carriers, diversifying its supplier base or changing its sourcing footprint, rather than relying on short-term fixes.

caseStudy.scenario: A mid-sized US retailer imports most of its consumer goods from Asia by ocean freight and holds relatively lean inventory. In November a trade outlook warns that carriers are cutting planned capacity, booking acceptance is weak and on-time performance on the lane is around one arrival in four. Management must decide how to protect product availability over the coming months without losing its cost advantage.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on how the retailer should manage the risk of constrained ocean capacity and unreliable arrivals on its Asia to North America lane, and critically evaluate whether the response should be temporary or permanent.
evidence: Capacity is expected to tighten because carriers are planning less capacity, not because demand is rising.
Booking security risk is well above its historical average and increases towards the end of the outlook.
Monthly on-time performance fell from 26.9% in September to 25.6% in October, with the latest weekly figure at 27.3%.
Delays of eight days or more are the largest arrival outcome on the lane.
plan: Diagnose the risk as a supply-side disruption, citing the reduction in planned carrier capacity and the rising booking security risk, and explain why it is not a demand problem.
Use Christopher and Peck's framework to identify the products and customers most exposed, and assess the cost of a stock-out against the cost of holding extra inventory.
Apply Cox's power analysis and Porter's bargaining power of suppliers to show why carriers currently hold leverage and why the retailer's dependence on preferred sailings weakens its position.

Evaluate the response options, including safety stock for critical lines, dual carrier or routing arrangements, and alternative modes or ports, using the cost-service trade-off to compare their total cost.
Judge from the outlook and the wider history whether the constraint is temporary or structural, and set out the implications for contract terms and supplier base.
Recommend a tiered resilience plan with specific triggers, such as booking acceptance or delay length, that would move the retailer between response levels.
pitfalls: Treating a single weekly on-time figure as a stable trend rather than noting the month-to-month movement and the tail of very long delays.
Recommending lean inventory reductions or simple price negotiation without considering that the constraint is on carrier capacity and reliability, which buying more cheaply does not solve.

exam.question: Critically evaluate how a global supply chain manager should build resilience against constrained ocean freight capacity, drawing on supply chain risk management theory and the trade-off between cost and service.
outline: Identify the supply-side source of the risk, using the evidence on planned capacity, booking security and on-time performance, and explain it with a resilience framework such as Christopher and Peck's.
Evaluate the main response options, including buffers, dual sourcing and alternative modes or ports, using the cost-service trade-off to compare their total cost and service effects.
Critique these responses, consider whether the constraint is temporary or structural, and recommend a resilience plan with clear triggers for action.

articles.title: Nearly half of employees fear being judged for not using AI enough at work
articles.takeaway: AI is raising productivity, but the time it frees is being absorbed into more work and higher expectations. For PWO, this is a question of motivation, the psychological contract and culture, not only of technology.
articles.summary: A survey of 3,001 professional employees worldwide, run by LSE and Protiviti, finds that 48 percent of employees worry about being judged for not using AI enough, against 20 percent who worry about being judged for using it. The share of respondents using AI at work rose from 29 percent in 2024 to 74 percent. Users report saving about 19 percent of their working week, but say they reinvest 72 percent of that time in other work. The authors call this 'workload creep': extra capacity is absorbed into existing duties or used to take on new responsibilities. Users also report real benefits, including faster task completion, less mental effort and better output quality. Dr Grace Lordan argues that leaders must direct where AI adds value and how saved time should be used, otherwise efficiency simply raises the baseline. The researchers recommend deliberate choices about reinvesting time in innovation, development, higher-value work and wellbeing.
keyPoints: 48 percent of employees fear being judged for not using AI enough, compared with 20 percent who fear judgement for using it.
AI use at work rose from 29 percent in 2024 to 74 percent in the 2026 survey.
Users save an average of 19 percent of their working week but reinvest 72 percent of that time in other work.
Half of those who saved time used some of it to take on new responsibilities or projects, and 65 percent spend more time on higher-value activities.
Users report faster task completion (82 percent), less mental effort (70 percent), automation of manual tasks (63 percent) and better output quality (62 percent).

modules.reading: This is a People, Work and Organisations story about how a technology change reshapes motivation, expectations and the unwritten relationship between employees and employers. The key question is whether the efficiency gained from AI is experienced as meaningful, rewarded or simply absorbed into heavier demands. Students should care because the article links motivation and engagement, job design, the psychological contract and organisational culture to current survey evidence.

From a leadership perspective, the article places responsibility on leaders to set direction about where AI adds value and how freed time should be used. The findings suggest that without clear direction, employees' expectations rise by default. This connects to leaders' role in clarifying the path to performance and to ethical and responsible leadership in how productivity gains are shared.

applications.theory: Job demands are the aspects of work that require sustained effort and can produce strain, while job resources are aspects that help people achieve goals, reduce demands or support growth. The model holds that demands and resources together predict wellbeing and engagement, and that high demands combined with low resources lead to burnout. Resources drive engagement mainly when they are not consumed by new demands.
applications.link: The article shows AI acting as a resource: 70 percent of users report less mental effort and 82 percent complete tasks faster. However, the 72 percent of saved time that is reinvested in other work, and the half who took on new responsibilities, show that the freed capacity is being converted into fresh demands. The researchers call this workload creep, meaning the resource is being used up by demand. The net gain in engagement that the model would predict may therefore be far smaller than the productivity figures suggest.
applications.critique: The model treats demands and resources as fairly stable features of a job, whereas here a single tool changes both at once and the employer's decisions about reinvestment determine the balance. It also says little about social demands such as the expectation to show AI use, which the 48 percent figure suggests is significant.
applications.practice: A manager applying this model should track workload as well as output and ask where time savings are going and whether employees are accumulating demands without more control. Deliberately reallocating some saved time to development or recovery would rebalance resources against demands.

applications.theory: The psychological contract is the set of unwritten beliefs that employees and employers hold about mutual obligations, such as the effort expected in return for rewards, security and development. It is shaped by promises, perceived norms and how people are treated. A perceived breach, where one party believes the other has failed to deliver, can reduce trust, commitment and engagement even when the formal contract has not changed.
applications.link: The article suggests the implicit bargain is shifting. Employees are expected to keep pace with AI and take on more, yet time saved is largely reinvested rather than returned as flexibility or reduced hours. Lordan's point that leaders must say where time savings go is effectively a call to make the implicit deal explicit. The 48 percent who fear judgement for not using AI enough suggest employees are reading an unwritten expectation that may not match what the organisation has actually promised.
applications.critique: The psychological contract is difficult to observe and measure. The article gives no evidence of what employers have promised or how employees' trust or commitment has changed. Fear of judgement may reflect anxiety about the technology rather than a belief that a formal or informal obligation has been breached.
applications.practice: A manager should make expectations explicit: state what AI use is expected, what counts as good performance and what happens to time saved. Revisiting these terms openly reduces the risk that employees experience an unacknowledged change in the deal.

applications.theory: Schein describes organisational culture at three levels: visible artefacts and behaviours, espoused values that people say they hold, and basic underlying assumptions that are taken for granted and largely unconscious. Shared norms about what is expected sit across these levels, and the deepest assumptions are the hardest to change. A gap between espoused values and observed behaviour signals cultural tension.
applications.link: AI use is becoming a visible artefact of working life, and the fear of being judged for not using it suggests a new norm is forming around it. The espoused values appear to be efficiency and better output, yet the assumption operating in practice seems to be that any freed time will be filled with more work. The article's call for deliberate decisions about the use of capacity amounts to a request to surface that assumption and examine it.
applications.critique: Schein's model is mainly a diagnostic framework and does not explain how a norm of technology use spread so quickly, from 29 percent to 74 percent in two years. The article also provides no direct evidence about the basic assumptions held by employers, so any reading of hidden assumptions is an inference.
applications.practice: A leader should compare what the organisation says about AI, such as valuing wellbeing and innovation, with what it actually rewards and measures. Where rewards favour output alone, changing performance measures and recognition is more likely to change the behaviour employees see as expected.

applications.theory: Path-goal theory holds that a leader's role is to help followers reach their goals by clarifying the path to desired outcomes, removing obstacles and providing support or rewards. The appropriate style depends on follower characteristics and task conditions, so directive leadership suits ambiguous tasks and supportive leadership suits high-stress situations. Leaders increase motivation by making clear the link between effort and valued outcomes.
applications.link: Lordan's advice that leaders be clear about where AI adds value and how freed time should be used is a direct example of path clarification. The article shows what happens without it: efficiency raises the baseline rather than delivering outcomes employees value. Employees who feel pressure to keep pace while their workloads rise are in the kind of situation where supportive behaviour is needed alongside directive clarity.
applications.critique: Path-goal theory assumes that clearer paths will motivate followers, but the article suggests that clarity alone is not enough. Leaders may lack control over budgets, headcount or performance targets, which determine how time savings are used. The theory also gives little attention to who has the power to decide how surplus capacity is allocated.
applications.practice: A leader should set out a clear purpose for AI use, specify the outcomes employees will be judged on and agree in advance how time savings will be allocated between new work, development and recovery. They should check periodically whether the path is supporting employees or simply raising expectations.

caseStudy.scenario: A professional services firm introduces AI tools across its consulting teams. Within two years most staff use them daily and managers report faster delivery of client work. Staff say they now complete more work in the same hours, and many feel they must show they are using the tools as much as colleagues, or risk being seen as behind.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate the claim that AI-driven efficiency gains will improve employee engagement. Advise the leadership team on how to manage the expectations that come with adoption.
evidence: 48 percent of employees fear being judged for not using AI enough, compared with 20 percent who fear judgement for using it.
Users save an average of 19 percent of their working week but reinvest 72 percent of that time in other work.
Half of those who saved time took on new responsibilities or projects, and 65 percent spend more time on higher-value activities.
70 percent of users report reduced mental effort, and 82 percent say AI helps them complete tasks more quickly.
plan: Define engagement, workload creep and the psychological contract, and separate the efficiency gain from the way employees experience it.
Apply the Job Demands-Resources model to show AI as a resource that is being consumed by new demands, so engagement depends on the balance between the two.
Use the psychological contract to explain the fear of judgement and the unwritten expectation to keep pace, identifying where the implicit deal may be breached.
Use Schein's three levels of culture to compare espoused values such as wellbeing and innovation with what the firm actually rewards and measures.
Evaluate the evidence: the survey reports perceptions and self-reported gains rather than measured engagement, and the benefits described are real.
Recommend that leaders agree explicitly how time saved will be used, reinvest some of it in development and recovery, revise performance expectations and set a clear path for AI use.
pitfalls: Treating the 82 percent who complete tasks faster as proof that engagement has improved, when the article reports efficiency and effort rather than engagement.
Presenting the 48 percent figure as evidence of actual unfair judgement, when it measures worry about judgement rather than recorded incidents.

exam.question: To what extent does technology that increases productivity improve motivation and engagement at work? Use theories of job design and the psychological contract in your answer.
outline: Define motivation and engagement and explain how job design and the Job Demands-Resources model predict the effects of reduced effort and added responsibility.
Use the psychological contract and Schein's levels of culture to assess whether employees' expectations and workloads are balanced when productivity gains are reinvested.
Critically evaluate the evidence, noting that survey data capture perceptions and self-reported gains rather than measured engagement, and recommend how managers should allocate saved time.

articles.title: Why AI skill-building is only one part of the puzzle
articles.takeaway: Treating AI adoption as only a skills or technology problem misses the people, workplace and cultural side of change, which is where many adoption efforts succeed or fail.
articles.summary: The abstract, summarising a Hogan Assessments report reported by HR Dive, says AI adoption is not just a technology challenge but also a people and workplace challenge. The title adds that AI skill-building is only one part of the solution. The abstract gives no figures, sample, method or detailed findings, so the note works from that framing alone and does not assume what the full report says.
keyPoints: The report frames AI adoption as a people and workplace challenge as well as a technological one.
The title argues that building AI skills is necessary but insufficient on its own.
The abstract gives no data, sample size or named findings, so claims about specific results should not be made from it.
The framing points to the wider organisational conditions (people, work design, culture, leadership) that shape whether AI tools are used well.

modules.reading: In People, Work and Organisations terms, the article is about the gap between installing a new technology and changing how people behave at work. Skill-building addresses ability, but adoption also depends on motivation, attitudes towards AI, job design, group norms and culture. A student of this module should see the piece as an argument that AI is an organisational change, not just a training exercise, and should be able to explain which people-related factors sit outside the skills agenda.

The leadership dimension is that someone has to set the direction for AI adoption, shape how employees understand it and make the case for changing working practices. The abstract's framing suggests that leaders who treat AI as only a technical project may miss the human side. A leadership student could use the article to discuss how leaders manage the people aspects of technological change.

applications.theory: ADKAR is a change model that sets out five outcomes an individual needs for change to succeed: awareness of the need for change, desire to take part, knowledge of how to change, ability to implement new behaviours, and reinforcement to sustain them. It is used to diagnose where individual change is stalling. Each stage is a precondition for the next, so the model is about people's progress through change rather than the change project itself.
applications.link: The article's point that AI adoption is a people challenge fits ADKAR's view that individuals must move through several stages. Skill-building maps mainly onto the knowledge and ability stages, but the abstract's wider framing implies that awareness, desire and reinforcement also matter. A manager could use the model to check whether a skills programme is being asked to do work that belongs to motivation, communication or workplace support. The abstract does not say which stages the Hogan report addresses, so the link is interpretive.
applications.critique: ADKAR is a practitioner model with limited independent empirical testing, and it presents the stages in a fixed order, which does not always match how people actually adapt. It also focuses on individuals and may underplay group and structural barriers.
applications.practice: A manager applying ADKAR would first assess employees' awareness and desire regarding AI before investing heavily in training. They would then match training to knowledge and ability gaps and set up reinforcement, such as feedback and performance expectations, to sustain new AI-enabled practices.

applications.concept: Schein's three levels of organisational culture
applications.theory: Schein describes culture at three levels: visible artefacts (such as tools, routines and physical settings), espoused values (stated beliefs and goals), and basic underlying assumptions (taken-for-granted beliefs that shape behaviour). Change is hardest at the deepest level. Introducing a new tool changes artefacts without necessarily changing assumptions about how work should be done.
applications.link: AI tools are artefacts that can be introduced quickly, but the article's framing suggests that adoption depends on people and workplace conditions that sit deeper in the organisation. If employees hold assumptions that expertise is personal and that automation threatens their status, skill-building alone will not change how they work. Schein's model helps a student explain why the people side of AI adoption is harder than the technology side.
applications.critique: Schein's levels are a diagnostic framework rather than a predictive one, so they can be hard to apply precisely to a specific organisation. Culture is also not always the main barrier, since structure, incentives and resources may matter more.
applications.practice: A manager would map the current AI-related artefacts, the stated values about AI, and the unspoken assumptions people hold about work and expertise. Interventions would then address the assumptions through leadership behaviour and shared norms, not just the tools and training.

applications.theory: The job demands-resources model argues that every job has demands (physical, psychological, organisational) that create strain when they are high, and resources (autonomy, support, feedback, development) that help people meet demands and stay engaged. Strain and engagement follow from the balance between the two, and resources can buffer the effects of high demands.
applications.link: AI adoption can add new demands, such as learning unfamiliar systems, checking AI outputs and adjusting workflows, while changing the resources available to staff. The abstract's emphasis on workplace conditions suggests that whether AI helps or strains employees depends on the resources around the training, such as time, support and a clear role. The model gives the student a way to explain why a skills programme alone may not reduce strain if demands rise faster than resources.
applications.critique: The model is broad and can be used to explain almost any workplace outcome, which makes it harder to test. It also tends to treat demands and resources as additive, while AI may change the nature of the job rather than simply adding to it.
applications.practice: A manager would audit the new demands AI creates for each role and check whether the resources (time, feedback, decision authority, support) are sufficient. Where demands exceed resources, they would reduce workload or add support before expecting full engagement with AI tools.

applications.theory: Transformational leadership, developed from Burns and extended by Bass, describes leaders who motivate followers to go beyond self-interest by articulating a compelling vision, providing individual consideration and stimulating intellectual engagement. It contrasts with transactional leadership, which relies on exchanges of rewards for performance. Transformational leaders are associated with higher commitment and change readiness.
applications.link: Because the article frames AI adoption as a people and workplace challenge, it implies that employees need more than instruction in new tools. A transformational leader could articulate why AI matters for the organisation, address concerns about the future of work and engage staff in shaping how it is used. The abstract does not describe leadership behaviour, so this is an application of the theory to the problem the article raises, rather than a finding from the report.
applications.critique: Transformational leadership is criticised for being hard to separate from charisma and for drifting towards a heroic view of leaders, which can neglect the structural and collective conditions the article points to. Its effects are also context dependent.
applications.practice: A leader applying this theory would set a clear, credible vision for AI that ties adoption to organisational goals and employee interests. They would involve staff in designing how AI is used and give individual support, rather than issuing mandates or relying only on training.

caseStudy.scenario: A mid-sized professional services firm has rolled out a generative AI tool to all staff and run a series of training sessions. Uptake is uneven, with some teams using it daily and others avoiding it, and managers report concern about job security and unclear rules on accountability for AI-assisted work. The board wants to know why the investment in skills has not produced consistent results.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate the view that AI adoption is primarily a skills problem, and advise the board on what else the firm should address to achieve consistent adoption.
evidence: The Hogan Assessments report, as summarised in the abstract, describes AI adoption as a people and workplace challenge and not only a technology challenge.
The article's title argues that AI skill-building is only one part of the puzzle.
The abstract gives no figures or detailed findings, so any firm-specific evidence in an answer must come from the case itself, not from the article.
plan: Define the problem using ADKAR to show which stages (awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, reinforcement) the training addresses and which it does not.
Use Schein's three levels of culture to explain why introducing the tool has changed artefacts but not the assumptions about expertise and job security.
Apply the job demands-resources model to identify new demands AI creates and the resources (time, feedback, clear accountability) that are missing.
Use transformational leadership to assess whether managers have articulated a credible vision and involved staff in shaping how AI is used.
Evaluate the limits of the case, noting that the abstract provides no data on the report's findings and that the firm's own data should be checked.

Recommend a combined package: clarify job-security concerns and accountability rules, redesign workloads to free time for learning, train managers as change leaders, and set up feedback and reinforcement.
pitfalls: Treating the abstract's framing as proven research results, or attributing specific statistics to the Hogan report that the abstract does not contain.
Recommending more training as the main fix without showing why the people and workplace factors make training insufficient.

exam.question: Critically evaluate the claim that technological change such as AI adoption is primarily a people and workplace challenge rather than a technical one. Use at least two models of organisational change or behaviour to support your argument.
outline: Define AI adoption as organisational change and explain why the people and workplace dimensions matter, drawing on ADKAR or Kotter's model of change.
Use Schein's levels of culture and the job demands-resources model to show how assumptions, demands and resources shape whether skills training leads to adoption.
Critically evaluate the claim, noting the limits of the abstract and the risks of overstating the people side while neglecting technology design, structure and resourcing.

articles.title: RTO policies that prioritize employees work better
articles.takeaway: Requiring staff to come into the workplace only works if being there is worth more to them than staying away, so a return-to-office policy should be judged by what it gives people.
articles.summary: The HR Dive piece, as far as the abstract shows, is a short commentary by Darlene Engoglia of Park Place Technologies. Its central point is that when an employer asks staff to come into the workplace, it should make sure that being there is valuable. The headline goes further and asserts that return-to-office policies which prioritise employees work better. The abstract gives no data, sample or measured outcomes, so the effectiveness claim should be treated as the author's position rather than a research finding. The full article may contain more, but this note works only from the abstract.
keyPoints: The abstract argues that an employer requiring attendance has a responsibility to make the time in the workplace worthwhile.
The headline claims that return-to-office policies which prioritise employees produce better results, but the abstract does not say what results or how they were measured.
The piece is an identified author's commentary from a technology services firm, not a report of research or of company data.
The argument is conditional: it accepts that employers may ask for attendance and focuses on the value of attending rather than on whether to require it.

modules.reading: In the language of People, Work and Organisations, the abstract is about how a demand for attendance affects motivation, engagement and the employment relationship, and about how a change to working arrangements is introduced. The author's point that attendance must be valuable rests on the idea that people comply more willingly when they can see a benefit, which connects to motivation theory and to the job demands and resources model. A PWO student should care because return-to-office disputes are a live case of organisational change, and the module's theories give structure to an exam or assignment answer. This reading is based only on the headline and one sentence of abstract, so the link is to the theory, not to any evidence in the article.

applications.theory: The model holds that every job has job demands, which are aspects requiring sustained effort or cost, and job resources, which help people meet goals, reduce demands or encourage growth. Demands tend to produce strain, while resources drive a motivational process that leads to engagement. The balance between the two determines how people experience their work.
applications.link: The abstract's requirement that office attendance be valuable can be read as a demand to supply resources. A required commute, set hours and loss of flexibility are demands that the employer imposes, and the office is only a resource if it provides things such as collaboration, coaching, social connection or access to equipment. The abstract does not name any such resources, so the mapping is an inference from its central claim. If attendance adds demands without matching resources, the model predicts strain rather than engagement, which is the outcome the headline seems to be warning against.
applications.critique: The model is largely a framework for organising variables and is mainly supported by correlational studies, so it cannot show that a given attendance policy will tip the balance either way. It also treats demands and resources as the employer's to adjust, whereas many commuting and caring constraints sit outside the workplace.
applications.practice: A manager applying this model should list the demands that attendance creates, such as travel time, cost and loss of flexibility, and the resources the office can offer that remote work cannot. Investment should then go into those resources, for example by scheduling in-person work that needs collaboration. Strain and engagement indicators should be tracked after any change so the balance can be checked.

applications.theory: Vroom's expectancy theory proposes that motivation depends on three beliefs multiplied together: expectancy, the belief that effort will lead to performance; instrumentality, the belief that performance will lead to outcomes; and valence, how much the outcomes are valued. If any one of these is zero, motivation falls away. Because the factors multiply, a weak link in any of them undermines the whole.
applications.link: The abstract's insistence that attendance be valuable maps closely onto instrumentality and valence. If the office is seen as the route to outcomes people want, such as better collaboration, faster decisions or career access, then attending is instrumental and valued. If staff see nothing they want at the office, the valence of attending is low, and a mandate adds compliance pressure without motivation. The abstract does not say which outcomes the author has in mind, so this application relies on reading its main claim through the theory.
applications.critique: Expectancy theory assumes people weigh outcomes rationally and individually, but attendance decisions are also shaped by fairness, caring responsibilities and cost, which the model handles poorly. It also does not explain how people respond when they feel coerced, as opposed to choosing to attend.
applications.practice: A manager should identify the outcomes that in-office work actually produces for each team and make those links visible, for example by scheduling in-person sessions for work that needs them. The manager should also ask staff which outcomes they value rather than assume, and adjust office days to match.

applications.theory: The psychological contract is the set of unwritten beliefs about the mutual obligations between employer and employee, which sit alongside the formal contract. A perceived breach occurs when the employer is seen to have failed to deliver something it implicitly promised, and this tends to reduce trust, commitment and effort. Changes to working conditions can alter these beliefs even where the formal contract stays the same.
applications.link: A return-to-office requirement changes what employees believe they owe and are owed, even if their formal contract is unchanged. The abstract's stress on prioritising employees suggests the author sees the mandate as a signal about what the employer values. If staff read the requirement as an imposition without reciprocal benefits, they may perceive a breach. The abstract does not report how employees actually reacted, so the breach reading is a possibility that the theory identifies rather than a finding from the article.
applications.critique: Rousseau's account concentrates on individual perceptions, which are hard to measure and can differ widely within one workforce. It also gives little guidance on how an employer should rebuild a contract once trust has been damaged.
applications.practice: A manager should make the implicit deal explicit by stating what the office is for, what the employer will provide in return, such as equipment, support or flexibility on other days, and by consulting staff before terms change. Where the contract is strained, the manager should look for early signs of withdrawn effort or lower trust and respond to them.

applications.concept: Kotter and Schlesinger's approaches to resistance to change
applications.theory: Kotter and Schlesinger identified six broad approaches to overcoming resistance to change: education and communication, participation and involvement, facilitation and support, negotiation and agreement, manipulation and co-optation, and explicit or implicit coercion. Each has trade-offs in time, commitment and the risk of later resentment. Managers are advised to choose an approach according to the source and degree of resistance.
applications.link: A return-to-office policy is a change to established working patterns, and the abstract's requirement that attendance be valuable points towards participation and facilitation rather than coercion. Simply mandating attendance corresponds to the coercive end of the spectrum, which the abstract implies will not work well by itself. The article does not describe how its policies were introduced, so the link is between the author's stated principle and the range of approaches the model offers.
applications.critique: The model treats change as a discrete programme with identifiable resistors, whereas hybrid working is an ongoing arrangement in which resistance can shift over time. It also gives limited guidance on how to handle a workforce that is divided by location, role or caring responsibilities.
applications.practice: A manager should diagnose the likely sources of resistance, such as commuting costs, caring duties or loss of autonomy, before deciding on an approach. Teams should be involved in deciding which days and activities suit the office, and negotiation should be used where particular groups have real constraints. Coercion should be a last resort because it tends to shift resistance rather than remove it.

caseStudy.scenario: An employer is considering requiring its staff to attend the workplace more often than they currently do. The HR director has been asked to advise the board on whether the policy will improve performance and engagement and on how it should be introduced. Staff views on the change are not yet known, and the business case rests largely on assumptions about collaboration.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on whether a return-to-office policy is likely to improve performance and engagement, and recommend how the policy should be designed and introduced.
evidence: The abstract states that an employer asking staff to come in should make sure that being there is valuable.
The headline asserts that return-to-office policies which prioritise employees work better.
The piece is a short commentary by a named author from Park Place Technologies, not a report of research findings.
The abstract gives no data on performance, engagement, sample size or method, so the effectiveness claim is unsupported within the text provided.
plan: Define the decision, identify the stakeholder groups affected and state that the evidence available is limited to opinion and assumption.
Use the job demands-resources model to set out the demands that attendance creates and the resources the office would need to provide to offset them.
Apply expectancy theory to test whether staff will see attendance as instrumental to outcomes they value, and identify which outcomes would need to be made explicit.
Use the psychological contract to assess how a mandate may be interpreted, and what reciprocal commitments the employer would need to make to avoid a perceived breach.
Use Kotter and Schlesinger's approaches to choose how the policy should be introduced, favouring participation and negotiation over coercion where constraints are real.
Recommend a phased approach: define the purpose of office days, consult and pilot with selected teams, then evaluate against agreed measures of performance and engagement before extending the policy.
pitfalls: Treating the headline claim that employee-focused policies work better as proven, when the abstract provides no evidence for it.
Arguing only for or against return to office without addressing the author's actual condition that attendance must be valuable, which is the central point of the abstract.

alsoConsider: Adams's equity theory (Unit 3 Motivation and engagement), for perceived fairness between office and remote staff
Hackman and Oldham's Job Characteristics Model (Unit 3 Motivation and engagement), for how office work is designed
Kahn's model of employee engagement (Unit 3 Motivation and engagement), for the conditions that make people willing to i
Lewin's three-step model and force field analysis (Unit 8 Organisational change), for the forces pushing for and against

exam.question: Critically evaluate the claim that requiring employees to attend the workplace improves their motivation, engagement and performance.
outline: Explain the mechanisms that could link attendance to motivation and engagement, using the job demands-resources model, expectancy theory and the psychological contract.
Assess the strength of the evidence for the claim and the conditions under which it may fail, including individual differences, perceived fairness and the possibility that the claim rests on opinion.
Recommend how an employer should design and introduce an attendance policy, drawing on change management approaches and on consultation with staff.

articles.title: AI, rising costs top list of 2027 talent concerns, per Gartner
articles.takeaway: Gartner's talent research, as summarised here, flags AI as a pressure on entry-level roles, which matters for PWO because it shows how an external technological trigger can reshape jobs, careers and the implicit deal between employer and newcomer. Only a one-line abstract was supplied, so the analysis rests on the theory rather than on findings from the full report.
articles.summary: The source is HR Dive's report of Gartner research on talent concerns for 2027, under a headline that places AI and rising costs at the top of the list. The only text supplied is a single sentence saying that Gartner researchers stressed the importance of entry-level workers, who are increasingly at risk because of AI. The abstract gives no figures, sample, method or recommendations, so this note does not supply any.
keyPoints: The headline identifies AI and rising costs as the leading talent concerns Gartner reports for 2027.
The abstract says Gartner researchers emphasised the importance of entry-level workers.
According to the abstract, entry-level workers are increasingly at risk because of AI.
The abstract provides no figures, methodology or specific examples, so claims about scale or mechanism cannot be made from it alone.

For PWO, the key questions are how AI changes job design for junior roles, what this does to the psychological contract with new joiners, and how learning and socialisation may shift when routine entry tasks are automated.

modules.reading: In PWO terms, AI is an external trigger for organisational change, and the article points to a specific effect: the roles most exposed are entry-level ones. Entry jobs are where people learn norms, build skills and begin careers, so reducing them affects both individual motivation and the organisation's future talent pipeline. A PWO student should read the headline as a question about how job design, psychological contracts and informal learning respond to technological change, not only as a labour-cost story.

applications.concept: Triggers for change: internal and external triggers, using PESTLE as a diagnostic
applications.theory: Organisational change is usually prompted by triggers, which can be external (such as technological, economic or legal shifts) or internal (such as performance problems or new leadership). PESTLE analysis is used to classify external forces so that managers can see which pressures require a response. Triggers differ in how urgent and how foreseeable they are, and that affects how change should be planned.
applications.link: The headline places AI and rising costs at the top of Gartner's 2027 talent concerns, which makes AI an external technological trigger alongside an economic one. The abstract's point that entry-level workers are increasingly at risk shows how a technological trigger can work through a specific group rather than the whole workforce. Mapping the article onto PESTLE, the technological factor drives the change and the economic factor shapes how firms will afford and justify it.
applications.critique: Triggers models tend to treat change as a response to a discrete event, whereas AI adoption is gradual and uneven across firms, so an organisation may not recognise the trigger until its effects are already embedded. Some sceptics would also argue that cost pressure rather than technology is the real driver, and the abstract does not settle which is more important.
applications.practice: A manager facing this trigger should separate the parts of the organisation that AI will change quickly from those it will change slowly, and should involve HR early in workforce planning. They should also test whether the entry-level roles being automated are the ones that still carry training and socialisation value, before deciding how to redesign them.

applications.theory: The psychological contract is the set of beliefs each party holds about the mutual obligations between them, including those that are not written down. It covers expectations such as development, fair treatment and job security in exchange for effort and loyalty. Breaches or perceived breaches of these expectations reduce commitment and engagement.
applications.link: If entry-level work is increasingly exposed to AI, graduates and junior staff may reasonably expect that their early roles will lead to skill development and a career path, yet the organisation may be automating the tasks that provided that route. The abstract's emphasis on the importance of entry-level workers suggests that the employer's own researchers see this group as strategically significant, which heightens the risk of a perceived breach if it is treated as expendable.
applications.critique: Rousseau's concept is largely about individual beliefs, so it can underplay collective or labour-market factors such as sector-wide reductions in graduate hiring, where individuals cannot negotiate the terms of the deal. The abstract also does not say how employers are actually responding, so any conclusion about breach is an inference.
applications.practice: A manager should identify which implicit promises junior staff currently rely on, such as training, progression and mentoring, and state explicitly how these will be preserved as tasks change. They should monitor engagement and intention to stay among early-career employees during the transition rather than assuming that a stable headcount means the contract still holds.

applications.theory: Every organisation has a formal structure of roles, reporting lines and procedures, and an informal organisation of networks, relationships and unwritten norms. The informal organisation often carries much of the real learning, communication and socialisation, and changes to the formal structure can disrupt it in ways that are not visible on an organisation chart.
applications.link: Entry-level roles are a conventional route through which newcomers learn the informal norms and networks of an organisation by working alongside more experienced colleagues. If AI reduces the number of such roles, the formal structure may look more efficient while the informal channels through which junior staff learn and integrate are weakened. This illustrates how a change to formal job design can have effects on the informal organisation that are not captured by headcount or cost measures.
applications.critique: The distinction is useful but somewhat static, and the informal organisation is not always a positive force; it can also perpetuate exclusion or resistance. The abstract does not describe how the roles are changing, so the argument that informal learning will suffer is a reasoned expectation rather than a finding.
applications.practice: A manager redesigning roles should map where informal learning currently happens, for example through peer networks and shadowing, and decide how those channels will be preserved if formal entry tasks are automated. Structural changes should be evaluated against both formal measures such as cost per output and informal ones such as knowledge transfer and integration.

caseStudy.scenario: A large professional services firm plans to introduce AI tools across its operations over the next two years. Much of the routine analysis and document work once given to graduate recruits can now be automated, and the firm is considering reducing its intake of entry-level staff. Senior managers believe the change is necessary to control costs, but the HR function is concerned about the effect on early-career development and retention.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate the people and organisational implications of the firm's plan to reduce its entry-level intake in response to AI, and advise the board on how the change should be managed.
evidence: The headline reports that Gartner places AI and rising costs at the top of its 2027 talent concerns.
The abstract states that Gartner researchers highlighted the importance of entry-level workers.
The abstract states that entry-level workers are increasingly at risk due to AI.
The abstract contains no figures, so any quantitative claim about the scale of the effect must be sourced elsewhere.
plan: Diagnose the trigger using PESTLE, identifying AI as the technological driver and cost pressure as the economic one, and assess how foreseeable and urgent each is (Unit 8).
Analyse the psychological contract with early-career staff, identifying the implicit promises of development and progression that the change may breach (Unit 3, Rousseau).
Examine how the formal redesign of junior roles affects informal learning and socialisation, drawing on the formal and informal organisation (Unit 6).
Evaluate the options available, such as redesigning rather than removing entry roles, and weigh cost savings against talent pipeline risk and reputational effects.
Recommend a phased approach that involves HR and staff in redesign, sets measures for engagement and retention among early-career employees, and reviews the decision as evidence accumulates.
pitfalls: Treating the abstract as evidence of how many entry-level roles will be lost, when it provides no such figure.
Presenting the change as purely a cost decision without considering the people, contract and informal-learning consequences that the PWO theory is designed to expose.

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that technological change such as AI should be managed primarily as a question of job design rather than as a question of organisational change.
outline: Define triggers for change and the contrast between technological and economic triggers, illustrating with AI and cost pressure.
Explain how changes to job design affect the psychological contract and the formal and informal organisation, especially for entry-level roles.
Evaluate whether a job design lens is sufficient, or whether it needs to be combined with change management models that address people's transitions and resistance.

articles.title: AI for Logistics: Why 81% of AI Projects Fail
articles.takeaway: Logistics firms are adding AI faster than they redesign the work around it, so returns depend on organisational readiness. Repeatable back-office tasks show clear gains, while customer-facing judgement work should stay human-led. The evidence comes from a vendor-sponsored study, so the figures need careful handling.
articles.summary: The article reports research by Lean Solutions Group and Everest Group, based on interviews with about 200 logistics leaders, which finds that many firms have moved beyond isolated AI pilots but few have redesigned their workflows. The CEO of Lean Solutions Group argues that firms should first decide which functions and tasks suit AI, and which still need human judgement and relationships, before automating. He cites back-office gains in invoice processing, track-and-trace, proof of delivery and email handling, and says carrier and customer sales should be augmented rather than replaced. The piece also promotes his company's expert-in-the-loop product, so its evidence is partly promotional.
keyPoints: 69% of firms have moved past isolated AI use, but only 19% have redesigned their workflows, which the article presents as the main reason for underperformance.
The headline says 81% of AI projects fail, but the body text says 81% of firms neglect the organisational transformation needed. These are different claims and should not be conflated.
30% of respondents reported below-expectation returns on AI investment, in a sector where freight brokerage margins are around 5%.
Firms without internal consulting capacity cycle through three or four technology vendors without a clear gain.
The article divides tasks into those needing human judgement and relationships and those that are repeatable, lower value and can be automated at low risk.

modules.reading: In the language of organisational behaviour and change, this article describes a technology-led change that stalls because the organisation has not been redesigned around it. The gap between 69% moving past pilots and only 19% redesigning workflows is a diagnosis of missing alignment between structure, processes, skills and people, rather than a technical failure. It bears on Unit 8 (change management and its people aspects), Unit 3 (job design, since the article sorts tasks into human and automated) and the staffing consequences of headcount reduction. Students should care because the article offers a current case for arguing that change fails through people and design rather than technology.

In project terms, the AI investments described are initiatives launched and then switched between vendors without a clear benefits plan. Firms cycling through three or four vendors while 30% report below-expectation returns points to weak benefits realisation and possible escalation of commitment. Students of Delivering Successful Projects should see it as an example of a technology project scoped around the tool rather than the business outcome.

For logistics operations, the article concerns freight brokerage, track-and-trace, invoice processing, route-deviation monitoring and proof of delivery, which are measurable operational processes. Its argument about which tasks to automate and which to keep human parallels decisions about automation and outsourcing in warehouses and transport networks. The thin brokerage margin shows why the balance between operating cost and service level matters in practice.

applications.theory: The 7S model holds that organisational effectiveness depends on the alignment of seven interdependent elements: strategy, structure and systems, plus shared values, style, staff and skills. A change to one element is likely to fail unless the others are brought into line with it. Managers should therefore diagnose fit before implementing change.
applications.link: The article says firms have applied technology without examining the fit and readiness of the organisation, including which functions suit AI and which tasks need human judgement.
