PESTLE sorts external forces into political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors. Identifying the trigger helps an organisation judge how urgent and how deep the change needs to be.
applications.link: The article describes several external triggers: the US Congress ending a 30 per cent credit for homeowners who buy solar while keeping the lease-based credit until 2027, the UK government deferring a decision on allowing heat pumps that the property owner does not own, and Indian guidelines for provider-led routes issued only in January 2025. Each is a political and legal trigger that changes which business model is financially attractive and so what installers and utilities must do. The industry survey in which 55 per cent of installers named third-party ownership as their most-used financing route shows that a trigger is already changing practice. The electrification target adds an environmental and economic pressure that affects the whole system.
applications.critique: Trigger analysis explains what prompts change but says little about how people inside firms respond, and the article suggests the policy environment is unstable, so firms may be adapting to rules that could reverse. Change models often assume a stable end state, which is unlikely while subsidy rules keep shifting.
applications.practice: A manager at an installer or utility should map each policy trigger and judge how likely it is to be reversed, separating reversible moves from commitments that are hard to undo. The move towards service models should be staged through pilot contracts, and the firm should plan how staff whose roles centre on selling equipment are supported through the transition.

caseStudy.scenario: A regional heat pump installer currently sells systems outright to homeowners, and some of its customers qualify for a government grant that goes only to owners. A new provider offers to install, own and maintain heat pumps for a monthly charge based on heat delivered, and the government is considering whether its grant should also cover such offers. The installer's board must decide whether to launch a service offer of its own.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board of the installer on whether to move part of its heat pump business to an energy-as-a-service model, and on how the government's subsidy rules should shape that decision. Critically evaluate the trade-offs and make a recommendation.
evidence: The UK Boiler Upgrade Scheme gives households in England and Wales 7,500 pounds towards replacing a fossil-fuel boiler with a heat pump, but requires the property owner to own the heat pump, and the government deferred a decision in November 2025 on allowing models in which the owner does not own it.
In a 2026 industry survey, 55 per cent of US installers said third-party ownership had become their most-used financing route.

The author cites estimates that about 78 per cent of California's rebate for rooftop solar reached households that bought their systems and about 153 per cent reached households whose systems were third-party owned.
A 108-home trial by Energy Systems Catapult found heat-as-a-service technically feasible but did not show it to be commercially viable.
plan: Define energy-as-a-service and distinguish it from equipment sales and from the older ESCO model, showing what changes for the customer's upfront cost and the provider's ownership risk (business model theory).
Use PESTLE to identify the policy shifts as external triggers for change and assess how reversible each one is (Unit 8, Organisational change).
Apply agency theory to the monitoring and credit-risk problem in household contracts, and explain how metering, guarantees and repayment through the bill could reduce it (finance).
Use Porter's five forces to test whether a subsidy paid to providers would lead to profit rather than lower prices in a concentrated market (strategy).
Apply service-dominant logic to the value proposition and pricing, noting the willingness to pay for protection against technical risk (marketing).

Recommend a staged approach: pilot service offers with business and fleet customers, press for an ownership-neutral or outcome-based subsidy, and build measurement of flexibility before scaling to households.
pitfalls: Presenting energy-as-a-service as proven to lower household costs or widen access; the article says the strongest case may lie in flexibility and that household evidence is thin, especially for heating.
Misreading the rebate shares as adoption rates; a share above 100 per cent means the price paid fell by more than the rebate, and the figures describe who received the subsidy value, not who adopted.

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether governments should subsidise the purchase of low-carbon equipment or pay for the carbon reductions and flexibility services that equipment delivers, drawing on the theory of externalities and market failure.
outline: Explain the unpriced externality and why it justifies public intervention, using Pigouvian and carbon-pricing logic.
Assess how the form of subsidy, owner-linked, ownership-neutral or outcome-based, shapes which business models emerge, citing the UK, Indian and US examples.
Evaluate the limits of subsidies, including unmeasured flexibility benefits, profit capture in concentrated markets and distributional effects, and reach a justified recommendation.

articles.title: Macroeconomic effects of rare earth supply disruptions
articles.takeaway: Small-value inputs can cause output losses far larger than their market value, so supply chain risk assessment must map production networks and criticality, not just spend.
articles.summary: Working only from the publisher's short abstract, this VoxEU column uses a network model to estimate the macroeconomic losses from a large, permanent shortage of rare earth elements. Although the market is small in value, the abstract says such a shortage can cause output losses far out of proportion to that value. For horizons under one year it reports GDP losses of 0.6% for the UK, 1.5% for the US and 1.8% for Japan. The authors argue that supply chain risk assessments should incorporate production networks, and that policymakers should build strategic reserves and develop domestic capacity. The mechanisms and assumptions behind the figures are not given in the abstract.
keyPoints: The rare earths market is small in value, yet shortages can cause output losses much larger than that value suggests.
A network model is used to estimate GDP losses from a large, permanent shortage over horizons of less than one year.
The reported short-run losses differ by economy: 0.6% for the UK, 1.5% for the US and 1.8% for Japan.
Supply chain risk assessments need to incorporate production networks, not only direct supplier relationships.
The recommended responses are strategic reserves and domestic capacity to withstand short-run losses.

modules.reading: The article treats rare earths as a supply chain risk in which an input of small value can stop output across connected sectors, because the shortage travels through production networks. For a student of SCM the key idea is that vulnerability lies in the structure of the network, not only in the value of the item. The abstract's recommendations, to map networks and to build reserves and domestic capacity, are standard resilience responses that can be assessed against SCM theory.

The article concerns securing supply of a commodity-type input that is cheap relative to total spend but critical to production. For a purchasing student this raises the question of how to classify and source items whose risk is not captured by price. The policy responses named in the abstract, strategic reserves and domestic capacity, are sourcing and supplier-development decisions that can be evaluated with purchasing portfolio tools.

For logistics operations the connection is through inventory control. A strategic reserve is in effect safety stock held at national scale, and the article's argument that value-based thinking misses the true risk bears on how inventory is classified and buffered. The abstract says nothing about transport or warehousing, so this is a secondary connection.

applications.concept: Supply chain risk management and resilience (Christopher and Peck)
applications.theory: Supply chains are exposed to disruption that spreads through interdependent suppliers, so resilience depends on understanding the whole network rather than only first-tier suppliers. Christopher and Peck argue that firms should map their supply base, identify critical nodes and build redundancy, flexibility and visibility to reduce both the impact of a disruption and the time needed to recover.
applications.link: The abstract argues that a shortage of a low-value input can produce output losses far beyond its market value, and that a network model is needed to see this. This matches the idea of hidden exposure beyond the first tier, where a firm may spend little on an input yet depend on it for critical products. The recommendation that risk assessments should incorporate production networks is a macro-level version of Christopher and Peck's call for network mapping. The headline figures, such as a 1.5% short-run GDP loss in the US, show how quickly such disruption can scale across an economy.
applications.critique: Christopher and Peck's framework is designed for firms managing their own supply chains and gives little guidance on how a government should weigh the costs of buffers across many firms. The abstract's results are model-based, and the assumptions behind them, such as the scope for substitution, are not described, so the precision of the figures should be treated cautiously.
applications.practice: A risk manager applying this theory would map suppliers beyond tier one for inputs with low spend but high criticality, identify single points of failure and estimate recovery times. They would then decide where to hold buffers or qualify alternative sources, giving priority to the nodes whose loss would halt the most output.

applications.concept: ABC inventory analysis and safety stock
applications.theory: ABC analysis ranks inventory items by annual value or usage and concentrates control effort on high-value A items, with lighter control for low-value C items. Safety stock is extra inventory held to absorb variability in demand or supply, and its size depends on the service level required and the uncertainty of lead times.
applications.link: The article's opening point is that the rare earths market is small in value, which would place such materials in the C category under a value-based ABC analysis. Yet the abstract says shortages cause disproportionate output losses. The call for strategic reserves is in effect a decision to hold safety stock for an item that value-based classification would under-control. The contrast shows that value measures spend, not the cost of a stockout.
applications.critique: Classification by value or volume ignores criticality and substitutability, so it misclassifies low-value but irreplaceable inputs. Criticality-based approaches such as VED analysis address this gap. Large national reserves also carry storage, obsolescence and opportunity costs, which the abstract does not quantify.
applications.practice: A logistics manager should classify inventory by criticality as well as value, so that low-value items whose absence would stop production receive higher service levels. For these items, safety stock should be sized to the expected length of an interruption, weighed against holding costs, and reviewed as supply risk changes.

applications.theory: Kraljic classifies purchases by profit impact and supply risk. Strategic items score high on both, leverage items are high impact and low risk, bottleneck items are low impact and high risk, and non-critical items are low on both. Each quadrant calls for a different sourcing approach.
applications.link: The article describes a market that is small in value but whose shortage causes large output losses, which places rare earths in the bottleneck quadrant: low spend but high supply risk and severe consequences. The abstract's advice to develop domestic capacity is a sourcing response to bottleneck items, aimed at reducing supply risk rather than unit cost. This shows that the matrix's placement of an item depends on the cost of disruption, not only on the price paid.
applications.critique: Kraljic's profit impact dimension is usually measured by spend, which is exactly the measure the article suggests can mislead. The matrix is also static and does not show how supply risk changes over time through substitution, new suppliers or policy shifts.
applications.practice: A purchasing director should reassess bottleneck items using the consequence of a stockout rather than spend alone. They should develop alternative sources, qualify substitutes and, where supply risk is structural rather than temporary, consider strategic inventory or domestic supply.

caseStudy.scenario: A national economy relies on imports of a few specialist materials that are small in value relative to total trade. A sustained, permanent shortage of these materials would reduce output in manufacturing and related sectors. Government and industry must decide how to assess the supply chain risk and whether to invest in strategic reserves or domestic capacity.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate the case for building strategic reserves and domestic capacity as responses to a permanent shortage of a low-value but critical input. Advise the government on its priorities.
evidence: Although the market for these materials is small in value, shortages can cause output losses far out of proportion to it.
Using a network model, the column estimates short-run GDP losses (under one year) of 0.6% for the UK, 1.5% for the US and 1.8% for Japan from a large, permanent shortage.
The column argues that supply chain risk assessments need to incorporate production networks.
It recommends strategic reserves and domestic capacity to help withstand the short-run losses.
plan: Frame the problem as a gap between spend and criticality: the input is small in value, but its loss halts output, which the bottleneck logic of Kraljic and the limits of value-based ABC analysis both help explain.
Map the production network to show how the shortage propagates to downstream sectors, applying Christopher and Peck's network mapping and risk identification.
Use the cross-country figures to show that exposure varies by economy, and explain why differences in production structure matter.

Evaluate the two responses in turn: strategic reserves as national safety stock, weighing holding and obsolescence costs, and domestic capacity as a sourcing diversification decision, weighing cost, lead time and the trade-off between single and multiple sourcing.
Critique the model's assumptions and the limits of firm-level frameworks applied at national level, noting that only headline figures are available in the abstract.

Recommend a sequenced policy: a criticality-based risk assessment across networks first, targeted reserves for the most critical inputs second, and domestic capacity where supply risk is structural, ending with a clear recommendation.
pitfalls: Treating the small market value as evidence of low importance; the relevant question is the cost of disruption, not the value of spend.
Presenting the model's GDP figures as definitive or as applying to all shortages; they relate to a large, permanent shortage under the network model's assumptions, which the abstract does not detail.

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether conventional supply chain risk assessments, which focus on the value of inputs and on first-tier suppliers, are adequate for protecting an economy against disruption to low-value but critical materials.
outline: Explain why value-based approaches such as ABC analysis and spend-based assessment understate the risk from low-value critical inputs, using the abstract's finding that small markets can cause large output losses.
Discuss the case for network-based risk mapping and resilience measures, such as strategic reserves and dual sourcing, drawing on Christopher and Peck and the abstract's recommendations.

Evaluate the limits of these responses, including the costs of holding reserves, the uncertainty in model-based estimates and the difficulty of building domestic capacity, and conclude with a prioritised recommendation.

articles.title: Where climate tech capital still goes and why
articles.takeaway: Climate tech capital is concentrating in a few firm-power and AI-linked companies that have paying buyers, while categories without a paying customer, such as carbon removal and low-carbon fuels, are being starved, so the choice of funding vehicle and customer matters more than the climate theme.
articles.summary: The article argues that climate tech funding in 2026 is being resorted rather than recovering. Money is flowing to firm power (fusion, fission, geothermal and storage) because data centre developers linked to AI need reliable electricity quickly and will pay a premium for it. Deal numbers are falling while the sums going to a few large firms rise. The author proposes five tests a funded category must pass: a buyer who must pay, revenue visible before the technology is finished, policy that survived, a visible exit, and a story framed as security or resilience rather than carbon. Carbon removal, low-carbon fuels and direct air capture fail several tests, and equity for carbon removal fell sharply in the first half. Debt shifted towards asset-backed project finance and then partly back to equity. The author says the climate return now sits in growth equity, infrastructure credit and project finance rather than early-stage venture, and that distressed or turnaround capital is a legitimate part of a mature ecosystem.
keyPoints: Firm power took about 6.3 billion dollars across 17 rounds in the third quarter, roughly 40 percent of climate tech equity that quarter, and was driven by demand from hyperscalers that cannot get firm power from the grid on their required schedule.
Data centre developers reportedly pay up to 150 dollars per megawatt-hour, roughly a 50 percent premium over a conventional new power contract, for clean, firm and quickly available power.
Equity funding rose in the second quarter while the number of deals fell to its lowest since 2021; in the first half, 10 deals took 42 percent of the money.

The author's five tests are a buyer who must pay, revenue visibility before the technology is finished, policy that survived, a visible exit, and a security or resilience story rather than a carbon story.

Carbon removal fails the buyer, revenue and exit tests; its equity fell 61 percent in the first half after Microsoft paused purchases and nature-based deals set a reference price near 20 dollars a ton.

modules.reading: This article is about how a capital-intensive sector is being financed, which is core finance module territory. It shows the trade-off between growth equity, project finance and infrastructure credit, each with different fees, liquidity and failure modes, and how staged funding is tied to offtake contracts. A finance student should see that the article treats funding as a sequence of decisions under uncertainty rather than a single valuation.

The article argues that the premium paid for clean firm power is the carbon price that climate tech never received from policy, which is an externality question. It also shows how a low reference price for nature-based carbon removal can leave engineered removal unfunded even when the environmental benefit is real. A green logistics or sustainability student should examine whether market prices are internalising emissions or merely rewarding reliability.

The article describes a market in which a small group of large buyers, mainly hyperscalers, holds the purchasing power over firm clean energy and offtake contracts. Their willingness to pay and their ability to anchor investment rounds shape which suppliers survive. A purchasing student should analyse this through buyer-supplier power and supplier dependence on a concentrated set of customers.

The article is mainly about capital and markets, but it describes organisations whose survival depends on a few external actors: customers, investors and governments. Resource dependence explains why a firm that relies on one buyer or one policy regime is exposed to that actor's decisions. The article also contrasts impact investors' values with market logic, which touches on how attitudes and values shape decisions.

applications.theory: A real option is the right, but not the obligation, to invest, delay, expand or abandon a project as uncertainty is resolved. Because flexibility has value, a static net present value can understate projects whose uncertainty will be reduced over time. Staged funding is one practical form of real options, since each tranche buys the chance to continue once specified risks are cleared.
applications.link: The article describes funding that arrives in stages: Nvidia signed a development deal before a valuation was set, and a Series B with an offtake behind it is treated as project finance with a longer runway. In option terms, the customer contract is the trigger that makes the next tranche worth exercising. First-of-a-kind geothermal wells and microreactors are long-dated options whose value depends on whether a buyer appears before the technology is proven. The article's tests can be read as a list of conditions that must be met before an option is exercised.
applications.critique: Real options assume that uncertainty resolves over time and that the investor can wait for information; here policy risk, such as the proposed cuts to nuclear and geothermal offices, and the narrowing of exit windows can close options before the uncertainty clears. Option valuation also struggles to price sentiment-driven withdrawal of capital, which the article shows can be as decisive as technical risk.
applications.practice: A manager valuing a first-of-a-kind climate project should model the investment as a sequence of tranches and define explicit milestones, such as a signed offtake or confirmed policy support, as triggers for each one. They should avoid committing the full capital requirement before the key uncertainties are resolved, and should test how far the option's value depends on exit conditions.

applications.theory: Cox argues that power in a buyer-supplier relationship depends on relative dependence: which party has more to lose if the relationship ends and which has credible alternatives. Scarce, critical supply gives a supplier power, while concentrated demand and few alternative sources give a buyer power. Managers can therefore analyse power by comparing the resources each side controls and how easily each could replace the other.
applications.link: Data centre developers can pay a premium because they cannot obtain firm power from the grid on their schedule, which gives firm clean suppliers real leverage in that segment. However, the article notes that capital is concentrating in fewer companies, nearly all selling to the AI buildout, so suppliers depend heavily on a small number of large buyers. The Nvidia and National Grid examples show the buyer also becoming an investor, which strengthens the buyer's hold on the supplier's future.
applications.critique: Cox's framework treats dependence as relatively fixed at a point in time, while in this market the balance shifts with each new round, each policy change and each new entrant. It also does not handle cases where the buyer's investment gives it control over the supplier's capital as well as its supply, which makes the relationship more than a purchasing one.
applications.practice: A climate supplier should diversify its buyers and avoid a dependence on one customer that cannot be replaced, using offtake contracts with clear pricing and step-in or exit terms. A buyer should weigh the security of firm supply against the fragility of a supplier that relies on it, and should consider whether taking an equity stake helps or harms its long-term sourcing position.

applications.theory: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on third parties and is not reflected in market prices. Carbon pricing, through a tax or a trading scheme, attempts to internalise the cost of emissions so that low-carbon options can compete on price. Without such a price, low-carbon activity depends on subsidies, voluntary purchases or the willingness of buyers to pay for other attributes.
applications.link: The article claims that the data centre premium for clean firm power functions as a carbon price that climate tech never received from policy, but the buyer is paying mainly for reliability and speed. Carbon removal shows the opposite problem: a reference price near 20 dollars a ton from nature-based deals is a fraction of the cost of engineered removal, so the environmental benefit is priced low. The article also notes that gas turbines bought as a bridge are being financed to run for decades, which illustrates how a market signal can reward a different attribute than the one a carbon price would target.
applications.critique: A premium for firm power is not a carbon price: it does not reflect the full emissions cost across the system and may reward fossil bridge capacity. Voluntary purchases also vary with corporate reputation and budgets, so they are an unreliable substitute for policy that applies to all emitters.
applications.practice: A sustainability manager should separate payments for reliability from payments for emissions reduction, measuring Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions for each sourcing decision. They should not treat a premium for firm power as evidence that carbon is priced, and should check whether any bridge capacity has a credible plan for retirement.

applications.theory: Resource dependence theory holds that organisations depend on external actors for critical resources, and the power of those actors is greater when the resource is scarce, important and controlled by few holders. Organisations respond by managing their dependence through diversification, buffering, contracts, or closer ties such as board seats or shared ownership. The theory explains why organisations often adapt to the demands of the actors they rely on.
applications.link: Climate tech firms depend on hyperscalers for revenue and on a small pool of investors for capital, and the article shows that concentration is growing: 10 deals took 42 percent of the money in the first half. The author notes that customers now appear in the capitalisation of companies, which turns dependence into ownership. Dependence on government is also visible, since nuclear and geothermal kept their tax credits through the rollbacks and the proposed budget still cuts their offices, so policy is another resource controlled by others.
applications.critique: Resource dependence explains why organisations accept external power but says less about how firms can also gain leverage, for example when scarce firm power gives suppliers bargaining strength. It is also largely structural and gives limited attention to the political tactics and coalitions that actors use to shape policy.
applications.practice: Managers of dependent organisations should map their critical resources and the actors who control them, then reduce dependence by finding alternative customers, investors or policy supporters. In the article's setting, a firm should seek a second customer or a second class of investor before accepting terms that bind its future to one actor.

caseStudy.scenario: A geothermal start-up has a working pilot and a letter of intent from one large data centre developer that will pay a premium for firm power. Its venture round is nearly spent, and public markets for comparable listings have fallen well below their highs. The board must decide whether to accept the anchor customer's terms, raise debt against future project cash flows, or take a discounted round from a turnaround investor.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on its funding and customer strategy, and critically evaluate whether it should accept the anchor customer's terms.
evidence: Data centre developers are reported to pay up to 150 dollars per megawatt-hour, roughly a 50 percent premium over a conventional new power contract, for clean, firm and quickly available power.
In the first half, 10 deals took 42 percent of climate funding, and low-carbon data centre developers alone took a third, up from 3 percent a year earlier.
Debt was roughly a quarter of climate funding in the first half, and asset-backed debt halved in the third quarter while equity rose.
Carbon removal equity fell 61 percent in the first half after Microsoft paused new purchases, and Fervo and X-energy shares are well off their highs.
plan: Diagnose the firm's position using the article's five tests: identify whether a buyer must pay, whether revenue is visible before the technology is finished, whether its policy support is secure, whether an exit exists, and whether its story is one of security or resilience.
Apply real options to show that the anchor contract is an option to be exercised in tranches, and recommend setting milestones for each tranche rather than committing all capital at once.
Apply resource dependence theory to assess how far the firm depends on one customer and a small group of investors, and identify how it could reduce that dependence.

Apply Cox's model of buyer-supplier power to negotiate terms that protect pricing, exit rights and supply commitments, and assess whether the buyer's equity stake would strengthen or weaken its bargaining position.
Compare debt secured on project cash flows with growth equity and a discounted turnaround round, weighing fees, control, liquidity and failure modes.
Recommend a staged funding plan with a second customer or investor layer, and state the conditions under which the firm should accept the discounted round.
pitfalls: Treating the data centre premium as proof that carbon is being priced, when the buyer is mainly paying for reliability and speed.
Assuming a discounted round signals failure; the article argues that a lower price for sound technology is the mechanism by which new capital enters.

alsoConsider: Capital structure theory (Modigliani and Miller; trade-off and pecking order theories)
Porter's five forces, particularly buyer power
Agency theory, for the divergence between investors' and managers' interests in staged funding

exam.question: Critically evaluate the claim that, for climate technology investment, the choice of funding vehicle matters more than the choice of sector or technology. Use real options and capital structure theory to support your answer.
outline: Define the funding vehicles (growth equity, infrastructure credit, project finance and venture equity) and explain how their risk, return, liquidity and failure modes differ, using the article's evidence.
Apply real options to explain why staged funding linked to offtake contracts changes the value of an early-stage climate project, and assess where the framework fails under policy and exit risk.

Reach a judgement on whether vehicle choice or sector matters more, weighing the article's finding that capital concentrates in a few firm-power companies against the view that the appropriate vehicle depends on the stage and customer position of each firm.

articles.title: Why Care Matters in Crisis: Leadership Insights from War
articles.takeaway: Leaders who express care in their language during a crisis are more likely to propose constructive rather than combative measures, so care is a leadership behaviour that can be developed and selected for, not just a personal trait.
articles.summary: The article reports a study by Stajkovic and colleagues of how 152 Israeli legislators used language during the Israel-Hamas war. Using text analysis and machine learning on over 5.2 million words, the researchers measured each leader's expression of care, a moral perspective that considers how decisions affect others. They also classified more than 4,000 policy suggestions as constructive (focused on cooperation and long-term solutions) or combative (focused on blame, punishment and escalation). Leaders who expressed more care made more constructive suggestions. Women used more care-based language consistently, and this difference helped explain why they made more constructive suggestions. Care language rose in the most intense periods of the war, and the gender gap narrowed somewhat, though women stayed higher overall. The authors argue that care can move crisis discussions towards better decisions, that the findings may extend to disaster response, humanitarian work and public policymaking, and that care-based leadership can be developed through scenario exercises, feedback and guided moral reflection. They also suggest selecting crisis-ready leaders by looking at their record of caring for vulnerable groups alongside conventional indicators of competence.
keyPoints: Leadership during crises is less studied than everyday leadership, although it may matter most.
Ethics of care leadership is the extent to which a leader expresses a care-based moral perspective, weighing how decisions affect others.
The sample was 152 legislators and over 5.2 million words of transcripts from Israel's national legislature during the Israel-Hamas war.
More than 4,000 policy suggestions were classified as constructive or combative.
More care in leaders' language went with more constructive suggestions.

modules.reading: This study is about ethical leadership in a crisis. The leader's moral perspective is measured through the care expressed in their language, and the outcome is the kind of decision they push for. For a leadership student the key point is that ethics is treated not as abstract principle but as an observable signal that shapes group decisions, and that the authors link this to selection and development. It also reminds us that much leadership theory is built on ordinary conditions, and the authors argue that high-strength events need their own evidence.

From the PWO angle the article touches on individual differences, including gender and the values and attitudes behind expressed care, and on power, politics and conflict, since legislative debate is a contest in which some proposals are combative and others cooperative. The question is how a person's values and framing of a problem shape the conflict dynamics of a group. Students should care because the study treats language and framing as observable markers of how people approach conflict, and suggests that a group's climate can shift from escalation to problem-solving.

The authors explicitly argue that their findings may apply to disaster response and humanitarian work, which is the core of this module. In humanitarian settings the dilemmas concern who receives help and how aid is framed when agencies, donors and governments are under pressure. The article suggests that the tone of leaders' arguments affects whether discussions move towards cooperative, long-term solutions. Students should consider whether care can be applied impartially across all those in need, which is the central test for humanitarian principles.

applications.concept: Ethical and responsible leadership and the ethics of care
applications.theory: Ethical and responsible leadership holds that leaders are accountable for the consequences of their decisions for the people affected by them, not only for results. The ethics of care, associated with Gilligan and Noddings, grounds moral judgement in relationships, attentiveness and responsiveness to others' needs rather than in abstract rules alone. A leader who expresses care shows this orientation in how they frame choices.
applications.link: The study operationalises this idea by measuring how much care appears in the language of 152 legislators during the Israel-Hamas war. Across more than 4,000 policy suggestions, leaders with more care-based language were more likely to propose constructive measures aimed at cooperation and long-term solutions rather than blame, punishment and escalation. This maps the theory's concern with consequences for others onto the difference between proposals that consider effects on people and those aimed at retaliation. Care is therefore visible in the content of decisions, not simply declared as a value.
applications.critique: The evidence is correlational and rests on language, which may be rhetoric or signalling rather than genuine moral commitment, since a legislator can speak of care while voting for escalation. The study also cannot show that care causes better proposals, because unmeasured factors such as party, constituency or personal experience may drive both.
applications.practice: A leader in a crisis should make explicit who is affected by each option, so that consequences for others are part of the debate and the record. Development can use scenario exercises and reflective feedback on how decisions are framed, and leaders should check whether their care extends to all those affected.

applications.concept: Functional and dysfunctional conflict (Pondy) and the Thomas-Kilmann conflict modes
applications.theory: Pondy argued that conflict can be functional, improving decisions and surfacing problems, or dysfunctional, when it damages relationships and diverts energy from the task. Thomas and Kilmann describe five modes of handling conflict, competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating, based on the balance between assertiveness (concern for one's own goals) and cooperativeness (concern for others' goals). Collaboration seeks solutions that meet the concerns of both parties.
applications.link: Combative proposals focused on blame, punishment and escalation resemble the competing mode and a dysfunctional spiral, while constructive proposals aimed at cooperation and long-term solutions resemble collaboration. The article shows that care-based language is associated with the constructive side, suggesting that the way a leader expresses concern for others can move a contested debate from competition towards problem-solving. The rise in care language during the most intense periods may also indicate that conflict pressure can prompt concern for others as well as hostility.
applications.critique: Legislative debate is adversarial by design, and some competition is functional because opposition scrutiny holds government to account, so a binary coding of combative versus constructive may oversimplify. The Thomas-Kilmann model concerns how individuals handle disputes, whereas the study measures proposals across a whole chamber, so the mapping is analogical rather than exact.
applications.practice: A manager facing a dispute should separate the issue from the people, state their own concern and ask about the other party's, and look for options that serve both sets of interests before choosing between escalation and compromise. They should watch for escalating language and reframe it towards long-term outcomes.

applications.theory: Social role theory holds that differences in how men and women behave arise largely from the social roles they occupy and the expectations attached to them, rather than from fixed innate traits. Expectations that women should be caring and nurturing are learned and internalised, and they can shape how people speak and act in public settings. Differences tend to shrink where roles and expectations become more similar.
applications.link: The article finds that women expressed higher levels of care-based language consistently, and that this difference helped explain their greater tendency to make constructive suggestions. Social role theory would read this as a product of socialised expectations about caring. The narrowing of the gender gap during the most intense periods could be consistent with that reading, since crisis may change which expectations of leaders are salient, although the article does not test this. The study therefore treats gender as an individual difference operating through a mediating variable, care-based language.
applications.critique: The study does not measure why men and women differ in care language, so social role explanations are not tested, and innate or personality differences in empathy could also account for the pattern. Treating gender as a group average also risks stereotyping individual legislators, since an average difference says little about any one person.
applications.practice: Organisations should not assume that care-based leadership is a women's trait or assign it by gender. Selection and development should assess care in individual leaders through their track record and behaviour, and encourage all leaders to use the framing habits associated with constructive decisions.

applications.theory: The core humanitarian principles are humanity (human suffering must be addressed wherever it is found), neutrality (not taking sides in hostilities or controversies) and impartiality (aid provided according to need alone, without discrimination). They guide how relief organisations operate in conflict and crisis. Care for people in need is the moral basis, but the principles require that care be applied equally to all affected people.
applications.link: The article argues that its findings about care in war may extend to humanitarian work and disaster response. The Israel-Hamas war setting shows care-based language operating in a highly polarised environment where proposals were either constructive or combative. The care that underpins humanity corresponds to the ethics of care measure, and the association between care language and constructive proposals suggests that humanitarian actors who frame decisions around those affected may move coordination towards cooperative solutions.
applications.critique: The study measured care toward whichever groups legislators referred to, and it does not show whether care was extended impartially to all sides, which the principles require. A care-based discourse that favours one community may be as divisive as a combative one, so neutrality and impartiality may be necessary checks on care.
applications.practice: Humanitarian managers in a crisis should frame communications and allocation decisions around need and the people affected, test whether their language is applied to all groups, and select field leaders with a track record of impartial care for vulnerable people. They should also use reflective exercises to check for bias in their own framing.

caseStudy.scenario: A national legislature is debating its response to an ongoing war, with proposals ranging from punitive measures and escalation to cooperative plans for long-term settlement. Researchers who analysed its transcripts found that legislators using more care-based language were more likely to propose constructive measures, and that care language increased during the most intense periods of the conflict. A government wants to build a pool of leaders for future crises and is considering how to choose and develop them.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate the claim that ethics of care leadership improves crisis decision making. Advise the government on how it should select and develop crisis-ready leaders.
evidence: 152 legislators and over 5.2 million words of transcripts were analysed during the Israel-Hamas war.
More than 4,000 policy suggestions were classified as constructive or combative, and more care in language was linked to more constructive suggestions.
Women expressed more care-based language consistently, which helped explain their greater tendency to propose constructive measures.
Care language increased during the most intense periods of the war, with some narrowing of the gender gap.
plan: Define ethics of care leadership and ethical and responsible leadership, explaining that care is judged by how decisions consider their effects on others.
Set out the evidence: the link between care language and constructive proposals, the mediating role of care in the gender difference, and the rise in care during intense periods.

Evaluate the evidence critically: the study is correlational, relies on language rather than behaviour, and covers one legislature in one war. Use social role theory to interpret the gender findings without assuming innate difference.
Apply Pondy's functional conflict and the Thomas-Kilmann collaborating mode to explain why constructive proposals are better suited to managing a contested crisis than competition and escalation.
Advise on selection: weigh a candidate's record of caring for vulnerable groups alongside conventional competence, and do not select on gender.

Recommend development through scenario-based exercises, structured feedback on how leaders frame decisions and guided moral reflection, with monitoring to check that care is applied impartially to all groups affected.
pitfalls: Treating the correlation between care language and constructive suggestions as proof that care causes better decisions.
Explaining the gender finding without considering social role expectations or individual variation, or recommending selection by gender.

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether ethical leadership grounded in care helps leaders make better decisions in crises, drawing on research into leadership during war and disaster.
outline: Define ethics of care and ethical and responsible leadership, and explain how care can be observed in leaders' language and decisions.
Evaluate the evidence, weighing the strengths of large-scale text analysis and the gender findings against limits such as correlation, language rather than behaviour, and a single context.
Conclude with implications for selecting and developing crisis leaders, including the need for impartiality and the risk of stereotyping by gender.

articles.title: Job applicants say they are using AI to discover, investigate companies
articles.takeaway: Candidates now research employers with AI tools, and what those tools surface can lead them to withdraw before applying, so an employer's image is shaped partly by what AI presents, not only by its own messages.
articles.summary: Based only on the publisher's short abstract, a new study reports that more than half of job candidates declined to apply for a role after learning about the company through artificial intelligence. The headline adds that applicants say they use AI to discover and investigate employers. The abstract does not say which tools were used, what information led candidates to withdraw, or how the study was conducted, so the finding rests on candidates' own reports and should be checked against the full article before it is cited in detail.
keyPoints: More than half of the candidates in the study said they had declined to apply for a job after learning about the company through AI.
Applicants report using AI both to discover employers and to investigate them.
The abstract does not say what information led to withdrawal, which AI tools were used, or how many people took part; these details must be checked in the full article.
The decision described happens before any application, so the employer loses candidates at the attraction stage, before recruitment processes begin.

modules.reading: In People, Work and Organisations terms, the article is about how prospective employees form perceptions of an organisation and what those perceptions do to their decisions. It also touches on culture, since candidates appear to judge what working there would be like from the information AI gives them. A student of this module should care because the finding shows that perception, expectations and cultural signals operate before any employment relationship exists, and that the organisation has limited control over the filter through which they are received.

Viewed from marketing, a company's employer brand works like a product brand in a labour market, and candidates' associations with it determine whether they consider it. The article suggests that information gathered by AI can change those associations and lead to a decision not to buy, in this case not to apply. A marketing student should care because it raises the question of how far a brand owner can manage associations that are now mediated by third-party tools.

applications.theory: Perception is the process by which people select, organise and interpret information about their environment, and it is shaped by their expectations, experience and needs. Selective perception means that people notice and give weight to information that fits their existing beliefs while filtering out the rest. Both processes mean that two people can receive the same information and form different views of it.
applications.link: The abstract shows candidates forming a view of a company from information gathered through AI, and then deciding not to apply, so their perception of the employer, rather than the employer's own account, drives the decision. The AI tool sits between the candidate and the company and selects, summarises and frames what the candidate sees, which means the candidate's perception starts from a filtered input. Because the abstract reports that more than half of candidates withdrew, the filter appears to have a strong effect on the outcome.
applications.critique: Perception theory locates distortion mainly in the perceiver, but here a substantial part of the filter sits in the technology, whose selection criteria are usually opaque to both candidate and employer. The theory explains how individuals interpret information but says little about how much the source of that information shapes the picture.
applications.practice: HR should check what the AI tools candidates use currently say about the organisation, identify which sources they draw on, and correct inaccurate or outdated material at its origin. It should also ask candidates who withdraw why they did so, so that it can distinguish misperception from genuine concerns.

applications.theory: Schein describes culture at three levels: artefacts, which are visible and easily observed, such as physical settings, behaviour and published documents; espoused values, which are the stated beliefs, strategies and goals; and basic underlying assumptions, which are taken-for-granted beliefs that are hardest to see and most powerful in shaping behaviour. Outsiders usually see only the first two levels.
applications.link: AI summaries of a company are likely to draw on the visible levels, such as reviews, public statements, reported policies and press coverage. A candidate who decides not to apply may be reacting to signals about what the organisation is like to work in, without ever seeing the underlying assumptions. The abstract's finding that over half of candidates withdrew suggests that these outsider signals are enough to change decisions.
applications.critique: Schein's model assumes that culture is revealed to insiders over time, whereas an outsider using AI receives a compressed and secondhand version that may misrepresent the deeper assumptions in either direction. The model does not address how external information intermediaries shape what an outsider takes to be the culture.
applications.practice: Employers should make sure that the artefacts and espoused values that AI tools can access, such as careers pages, responses to reviews and leaders' public communications, match actual practice. A gap between stated and lived values is what an outsider is most likely to pick up as a warning sign, so closing it protects the employer brand.

applications.theory: The psychological contract is an individual's beliefs about the mutual obligations between themselves and their employer, such as what they will give and what they expect in return. It is formed from promises, expectations and perceptions of the relationship rather than from written terms alone. Breaches occur when the individual believes the employer has failed to honour these obligations.
applications.link: Candidates who decide not to apply after learning about a company through AI are forming expectations about obligations before any formal contract exists. If what they find suggests that the employer would not meet their expectations on development, workload or fairness, the psychological contract is never formed. This illustrates that the contract begins at the attraction stage, not at hiring.
applications.critique: Rousseau's work concerns the contract within an existing employment relationship, so applying it to pre-hire decisions stretches the concept. The abstract gives no evidence about which expectations candidates held or whether they were accurate.
applications.practice: HR should treat recruitment messaging as part of the psychological contract by describing development opportunities, workload and flexibility accurately. Mismatched expectations created at recruitment damage trust later, so accurate messaging protects both attraction and retention.

applications.theory: Keller's customer-based brand equity model holds that brand value comes from what customers know and think about a brand, namely its awareness and its associations. Equity is strongest when associations are favourable, strong and unique, and it can be weakened by negative associations that lead customers to reject the brand.
applications.link: An employer brand works like a product brand in a labour market, and a candidate's knowledge of the company, gathered through AI, forms associations that either add to or subtract from its equity. The finding that more than half of candidates declined to apply after this research shows a negative association leading directly to rejection of the offer before it is made.
applications.critique: Keller's model assumes the brand owner can shape associations through its own marketing, whereas AI now mediates many associations and the owner has limited control over them. The model was developed for consumer products, and job candidates face different constraints and switching costs.
applications.practice: Employers should map the associations that candidates form from the sources AI draws on, define the associations they want, and measure awareness and favourability among candidates rather than relying only on application volumes.

caseStudy.scenario: A company in this position has found that many candidates who research it with AI tools go no further in the application process. Its recruitment team does not know what those tools say about the organisation or which sources they use. The company wants to understand why candidates withdraw and what it should change.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate how an organisation should respond when candidates decline to apply after researching it through AI. Advise the HR director on the actions to take.
evidence: The study reports that more than half of candidates declined to apply for a job after learning about a company through artificial intelligence.
Applicants say they use AI to discover and investigate companies.
The abstract does not state which information caused withdrawal, so the answer should treat the causes as a question to investigate, not as established fact.
plan: Define the problem using perception theory: candidates form a view of the company from an AI-filtered picture, so the employer's own messages are not the only input.
Use Schein's three levels to explain which signals candidates can see (artefacts and espoused values) and which they cannot (underlying assumptions), and why this gap matters.
Apply the psychological contract to show that expectations formed at the attraction stage can end the relationship before it starts.
Use Keller's brand equity model to frame the employer brand and the negative associations that lead to withdrawal.
Critically assess the limits of these models, including the opacity of AI tools and the lack of detail in the evidence available.
Recommend an audit of what AI tools say, alignment of stated and lived values, accurate recruitment messaging, and structured feedback from candidates who withdraw.
pitfalls: Stating which tools, which information or which sectors the study covered, which the abstract does not provide.
Treating AI as a neutral information source, when the answer should recognise that its selection and framing shape candidates' perceptions.

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that organisations can no longer control how they are perceived by prospective employees, and discuss the implications for managing culture and people at the point of recruitment.
outline: Define perception, selective perception and the psychological contract, and explain how each operates before employment begins.
Use the finding that over half of candidates declined to apply after AI research, noting that the abstract does not say what candidates learned.
Evaluate the limits of organisational control over AI-mediated information and recommend actions that align stated and lived culture with accurate recruitment messages.

articles.title: Week in review: Can AI root out manager bias?
articles.takeaway: The headline question, whether AI can root out manager bias, is a People, Work and Organisations question about perception, judgement and evaluation. The abstract reports no findings, so treat this as a prompt to read the full stories before using them as evidence.
articles.summary: This is a weekly roundup from HR Dive. The publisher's abstract says it covers a single case and its effect on diversity and inclusion programming, and how artificial intelligence is affecting jobs. The headline asks whether AI can root out manager bias. Because only the abstract is available, the note cannot report what the articles conclude. It can, however, show how the headline question maps onto the theory of perception, individual differences and performance management.
keyPoints: The abstract gives no findings, figures or named examples, so nothing about the cases or AI tools can be reported as fact.
The headline frames AI as a possible remedy for manager bias, which raises the question of whether a tool can correct a human bias it may have learned from human decisions.
Perceptual biases such as stereotyping, the halo effect and selective perception are the classic mechanisms by which managers' judgements of people become distorted.
A single case affecting diversity and inclusion programming suggests that how an organisation responds to one incident can shape the wider culture and the credibility of its programmes.
Any claim that AI removes bias needs checking against what data the tool was trained on and who reviews its outputs.

modules.reading: In the language of PWO this is a question about perception and judgement in individual differences, specifically whether the biases managers bring to decisions about people such as hiring, appraisal and promotion can be reduced. The headline suggests the answer may depend on whether AI is used to replace or to check human judgement. A PWO student should care because these biases are a standard part of Unit 2 and a central concern in Unit 3 performance management.

For leadership, the question concerns decision making and ethical responsibility: if a manager relies on an AI tool, who is accountable for a biased outcome? The single case mentioned in the abstract touches on how leaders respond when diversity commitments are tested. Students of leadership should consider whether delegating judgement to a tool changes the leader's duty to ensure fair treatment.

applications.concept: Perceptual biases: halo effect, stereotyping and selective perception
applications.theory: Perception is an active process in which people select and interpret information through their existing beliefs and expectations. Biases such as the halo effect (one positive trait colouring the whole judgement), stereotyping (judging people by group membership) and selective perception (attending only to information that fits a view) distort evaluations of individuals.
applications.link: The headline asks whether AI can root out manager bias, which places the bias in the manager's perception of people rather than in the process alone. If AI is positioned as a way to strip out these distortions, the test is whether it reduces stereotyping and selective attention in the decisions the article covers. The abstract does not say how the tools are used, so the student should check whether the AI replaces the manager's judgement or simply supplies information the manager still interprets.
applications.critique: Perceptual biases are not only in the individual; they can be built into the data and criteria an AI tool learns from, so a tool trained on past decisions can reproduce the bias it is meant to remove. Perception theory alone does not explain how bias is transferred into algorithms.
applications.practice: A manager who wants to use AI for people decisions should first identify which biases are most likely in the decision, such as stereotyping in promotion. They should then test the tool's outputs against comparable human decisions and keep a human review step where judgement is still needed.

applications.theory: Performance management is the continuous process of setting goals, monitoring performance, giving feedback and making decisions about reward and development. Its fairness depends on the accuracy and consistency of the appraisal, and biased ratings undermine both motivation and perceived justice.
applications.link: If AI tools are used to assess or rank employees, the headline's concern becomes a performance management issue: whether ratings and decisions about pay or progression are accurate and consistent across groups. The abstract's mention of AI affecting jobs suggests that the same tools may also influence who is hired or retained. The student should look for evidence on whether the tool's assessments are checked against outcomes and whether employees can challenge them.
applications.critique: Performance management models assume managers can observe and rate performance accurately, which the bias literature questions. Applying AI without clear performance criteria may simply automate a poorly defined appraisal process.
applications.practice: Before deploying a tool, define the performance criteria in observable terms, audit the ratings by group, and give employees feedback on how their assessment was reached. Managers should be trained to question AI outputs rather than accept them as neutral.

applications.theory: Ethical and responsible leadership holds that leaders are accountable for the fairness and consequences of decisions they make or delegate, and for setting the moral standards others follow. The leader's responsibility does not transfer to a tool or to subordinates.
applications.link: Where AI is used in decisions about people, the headline raises the question of accountability: a biased outcome from an algorithm is still an outcome the organisation must answer for. The single case in the abstract shows that how leaders respond to a diversity failure can determine whether their commitments are believed. The student should identify who is named as responsible for the tool's decisions in the full article.
applications.critique: Ethical leadership theory describes what leaders should do but offers little guidance on how accountability works when decisions are distributed between people and systems. Responsibility can become diffuse, which is a practical gap the theory does not close.
applications.practice: A leader should name an accountable owner for any AI tool used in people decisions, require regular bias audits, and report the results openly. Where a case damages trust in diversity programmes, the leader should respond with specific actions rather than statements.

caseStudy.scenario: A large employer introduces an AI tool to support promotion decisions after a single publicised case damaged confidence in its diversity and inclusion programme. Managers still make the final decisions, but the tool ranks candidates and flags concerns. Staff in some groups report that they feel overlooked, and the HR team is unsure whether the tool is reducing or repeating manager bias.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate whether AI can reduce manager bias in promotion decisions, and advise the HR director on the steps needed before the tool is extended to appraisal.
evidence: The HR Dive roundup headline asks whether AI can root out manager bias.
The abstract states that a single case has affected diversity and inclusion programming.
The abstract states that artificial intelligence is affecting jobs, which suggests the tools bear on people decisions.
These are headlines only; the full articles must be checked before any finding is cited.
plan: Define the relevant perceptual biases (halo effect, stereotyping, selective perception) and explain how they distort promotion decisions.
Assess whether the AI tool removes these biases or only moves them into its data and criteria, drawing on the point that tools trained on past decisions can reproduce them.
Apply performance management theory to ask whether the criteria used for ranking are observable, consistent and fairly measured.
Apply ethical and responsible leadership to identify who is accountable for biased outcomes and how trust can be rebuilt after the case.
Recommend a bias audit by group, a human review step and transparent criteria before the tool is extended to appraisal.
pitfalls: Stating that AI removes bias without testing the tool's data and outputs, which the abstract does not support.
Presenting the headlines as findings rather than as prompts to be checked against the full articles.

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether artificial intelligence can reduce bias in managers' decisions about people, drawing on theories of perception and individual differences.
outline: Define perceptual biases such as the halo effect, stereotyping and selective perception, and explain how they distort evaluations.
Assess whether AI tools remove these biases or transfer them through the data and criteria they use, with reference to the accountability of managers.
Conclude with conditions under which AI can support fairer decisions, such as bias audits, human review and transparent criteria.

articles.title: Many executives say they are worried about leading with empathy
articles.takeaway: When pressure to invest heavily in AI grows, executives may deprioritise employee well-being, culture and retention. Psychological contract, job demands-resources and culture theory from PWO explain why that trade-off can cost the engagement the AI programme depends on.
articles.summary: According to the publisher's abstract, which reports Businessolver's findings, C-suite executives facing pressure to make decisive AI investments are pushing employee well-being, organisational culture and retention down their list of priorities. The headline adds that many executives are uneasy about leading with empathy. The abstract gives no figures, sample or method, so the scale of the trend and the reasons behind it cannot be judged from it.
keyPoints: Pressure to commit heavily to AI is leading senior executives to deprioritise employee well-being.
Culture and retention are also being moved down the agenda, according to the same source.
The headline reports that many executives are worried about leading with empathy.
The abstract is brief and gives no sample size, data or method, so the extent of the trend is unclear.

modules.reading: In PWO terms this is about how top-level priorities shape the employee experience. Well-being, culture and retention sit at the centre of Unit 3 (engagement and the psychological contract) and Unit 7 (organisational culture), and the abstract suggests they are being traded away for technology investment. A PWO student should care because it shows how strategic choices can change motivation, identity and intention to stay, and it gives material to test theory against.

This is a leadership question about empathy, responsibility and the choices leaders make under pressure. Emotional intelligence and ethical leadership frameworks suggest that leaders who attend to people's needs will act differently when resources are tight. The headline raises whether leaders feel able to show empathy when competitive pressure is high, which matters for anyone studying leadership practice.

applications.theory: The psychological contract is the set of unwritten beliefs that employees and employers hold about mutual obligations, such as effort in return for support, development and security. When one party seems to fall short of these expectations, employees may perceive a breach, which reduces trust and commitment.
applications.link: The abstract says executives are deprioritising well-being, culture and retention while pursuing AI investment. Employees may read reduced attention to their well-being and retention as a sign that the organisation is no longer keeping its side of an implicit deal, so the trend maps onto the mechanism of perceived breach. The abstract does not report employee reactions, so this is an inference rather than a finding.
applications.critique: Rousseau's framing focuses on individual perceptions and may underplay structural causes such as investor pressure or cost constraints. It also does not say which expectations matter most to staff, so managers cannot easily tell which breaches will do the most damage.
applications.practice: Managers should identify which expectations matter most to their people and explain openly why priorities are shifting. They should also protect the visible parts of the deal, such as development opportunities and well-being support, so that employees can see the organisation still honours its commitments.

applications.theory: The job demands-resources model proposes that job demands, such as workload, pressure and change, drain energy and can lead to burnout. Job resources, such as support, autonomy, feedback and recognition, foster engagement and motivation and can buffer the effect of demands.
applications.link: AI-driven pressure to win bets increases demands on executives and probably on staff, while the abstract says well-being support and culture, which act as resources, are being deprioritised. On the model, demands rising as resources fall is a risky combination for engagement. The abstract does not measure demands or resources, so the application is a hypothesis to test rather than a conclusion.
applications.critique: The model tends to treat resources as relatively stable, whereas in practice they can be cut quickly when budgets tighten. It also does not say how long a resource deficit can be sustained before engagement falls, which limits its use for forecasting.
applications.practice: Before cutting people-focused programmes, a manager should audit the main demands created by the AI programme and the resources available to meet them. They should protect the resources that buffer the heaviest demands and monitor indicators of burnout and engagement as the programme proceeds.

applications.theory: Schein distinguishes three levels of culture: visible artefacts, espoused values that are stated, and basic underlying assumptions that are taken for granted. Changing culture requires working at the deeper levels, and a gap between espoused values and actual behaviour suggests that the stated culture is not fully held.
applications.link: The abstract suggests executives say people and culture matter but deprioritise them when AI pressure arrives. The gap between what leaders espouse and what they fund and give attention to matches the espoused-versus-enacted gap Schein describes. The headline's reference to worry about leading with empathy may point to underlying assumptions about what leadership should look like, though the abstract does not say what those assumptions are.
applications.critique: Schein's model describes culture more clearly than it explains why such gaps arise. Competing views, such as the Competing Values Framework or power-based accounts, would put more weight on incentives, politics and whose priorities win budget battles.
applications.practice: Leaders should test whether their decisions match their stated values, for example by checking where budget and leadership time actually go. They should also link AI targets to measures of culture and well-being so that the people dimension is tracked alongside technology returns.

applications.theory: Goleman argues that emotional intelligence, including self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skill, is an important leadership capability. He links it to effectiveness, particularly when leaders are guiding people through change.
applications.link: The headline's concern with leading with empathy maps onto the empathy dimension of emotional intelligence, and the abstract suggests executives may see empathy as costly under AI pressure. Goleman would frame empathy as a learnable skill that supports change rather than as a soft extra. The abstract does not report what executives actually think or do, so the link rests on the headline alone.
applications.critique: Goleman's claims about the predictive power of emotional intelligence have been contested, with some researchers arguing that the evidence is weak or overstated. Empathy on its own also does not guarantee good decisions, so it needs to be combined with commercial judgement.
applications.practice: Leaders should build empathy into their decision routines, for example by asking how a proposed change will affect people before approving it. They should develop it through feedback and coaching rather than treating it as optional.

caseStudy.scenario: A company in this position has committed heavily to AI and faces board pressure for fast returns. Its executives are considering cuts to well-being, culture and retention spending to fund the programme. Some senior leaders are reported to be uneasy about showing empathy during the transition.
caseStudy.question: Advise the executive team on whether to protect spending on employee well-being, culture and retention while pursuing its AI programme. Critically evaluate the trade-offs.
evidence: According to Businessolver, as reported by the publisher, executives under pressure to pursue AI investment are deprioritising employee well-being, culture and retention.
The headline states that many executives are worried about leading with empathy.
The abstract gives no figures, sample or method, so any evidence drawn from it should be presented as indicative only.
plan: Define the problem as a trade-off between short-term AI returns and the people resources that sustain performance, and use the psychological contract (Rousseau) to frame employee expectations.
Apply the job demands-resources model to show how AI-driven demands could erode engagement if support and development resources are cut.
Use Schein's levels of culture to test whether the stated values match what the executive team actually funds and prioritises.
Apply Goleman's emotional intelligence to explain why empathetic leadership supports change, and address executives' concerns about it.
Assess the options of protecting, cutting or redirecting budgets against the evidence, noting the limits of a brief abstract.
Recommend a course of action: protect core retention and well-being resources, link AI targets to people measures, and communicate the rationale openly.
pitfalls: Treating the abstract's findings as established fact; a strong answer says they come from a brief summary with no stated method or data.
Describing empathy as merely soft; a strong answer shows how it links to engagement, retention and change outcomes through named theory.

alsoConsider: Cameron and Quinn's Competing Values Framework

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that organisations which deprioritise employee well-being and culture during technological change will undermine the engagement and retention they need to realise the benefits of that change.
outline: Explain the psychological contract and the job demands-resources model to show how well-being and retention relate to engagement.
Use Schein's levels of culture to assess the gap between stated values and resource decisions, citing evidence from the article.
Critically evaluate the claims, noting the limits of a brief source and alternative explanations such as cost and investor pressure, then reach a balanced recommendation.

articles.title: ISG: Manufacturers in North American are strengthening factory resilience
articles.takeaway: North American manufacturers are making factory resilience a design problem, restructuring regional production and supply networks while modernising ageing plants without stopping production. For PWO, the same article shows that technology change depends on people: skills, oversight and support in live operations.
articles.summary: The article reports on an ISG study, the 2026 ISG Provider Lens Manufacturing Industry Services and Solutions report, which says North American manufacturers are strengthening factory resilience. They are restructuring regional production and supply networks to keep output going despite trade-policy shifts, economic uncertainty and supply disruptions. Manufacturers are also coordinating product, plant and service workflows to protect safety, continuity and traceability. Ageing plants and regional supplier networks make this coordination harder, so firms are pursuing AI deployment and brownfield modernisation while also addressing workforce skills and local support. The article says technology must fit ageing assets, skill shortages and live production, and that AI applications need simulation, human oversight, safety assurance and rollback-tested deployment before they affect physical operations. Supply chain control towers are being given supplier, inventory, transport and plant constraints to improve regional traceability, and aftermarket programmes link connected-asset data, spare-parts planning, field service and reverse logistics. The article gives no quantified results. The headlines listed after the main text are unrelated and have been ignored.
keyPoints: Manufacturers are restructuring regional production and supply networks in response to trade-policy shifts, economic uncertainty and supply disruptions, so resilience is being built into network design.
Ageing plants and regional supplier networks make coordination of product, plant and service workflows especially important.
Technology decisions are driven by operational continuity: solutions must fit ageing assets, skill shortages and live production environments.

Physical AI in plants (machine vision, adaptive process control, autonomous material movement, predictive maintenance) must pass simulation, human oversight, safety assurance and rollback-tested deployment first.
Control towers are being extended to show supplier, inventory, transport and plant constraints, which supports regional traceability.

modules.reading: The article is about supply chain resilience: manufacturers are changing the geography of production and supply networks to absorb trade-policy shocks and supply disruptions. Students of SCM should see this as a shift from pure cost efficiency towards designing for risk, with regional sourcing, better visibility through control towers and tighter coordination across tiers.
